Article Title: California is set to break ground on a project to transform 2,800 acres of Delta farmland on Webb Tract into wetlands and rice fields, reversing decades of land subsidence while creating habitat and s
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Why Webb Tract is being transformed

How wetlands and rice can help slow subsidence

Restoring habitat while storing carbon

A $28 million project with broader goals

California is moving ahead with a major restoration project that will reshape about 2,800 acres of farmland on Webb Tract in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta into wetlands and upland habitat, alongside rice cultivation. According to the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California and the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta Conservancy, the project is intended to address decades of land subsidence while reducing greenhouse gas emissions, storing carbon and creating habitat for wildlife. The approximately $28 million project is being supported by a $20.9 million grant from the Delta Conservancy, with Metropolitan covering the remaining cost.Webb Tract is a Metropolitan-owned island in Contra Costa County, located within the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, a region that supports agriculture, communities and a major part of California's water supply. But the landscape has also been affected by decades of conventional farming. For more than a century, much of the Delta's farmland has been managed by draining the soil to grow crops. This has affected the peat soils beneath the islands.Once these organic-rich soils are drained and exposed to air, they can break down and cause the land surface to gradually sink, a process known as land subsidence.According to Metropolitan, some areas of the Delta have subsided to as much as 24 feet below sea level. On Webb Tract, the restoration strategy is therefore centred on putting water back onto the landscape rather than continuing to rely entirely on dry-soil farming. The project will restore approximately 2,800 acres of wetlands and upland habitat. At the same time, agricultural land on Webb Tract is being converted to rice cultivation, creating a landscape that combines farming with environmental restoration.The key to the project is keeping the peat soil wet. When peat remains waterlogged, it has less exposure to oxygen, which slows the decomposition of organic material. That can help prevent further loss of soil and, under suitable conditions, allow the land surface to gradually rebuild through the accumulation of organic material. Rice farming fits into this approach because rice is cultivated in wet conditions. Metropolitan has previously said it leased more than 2,100 acres of Webb Tract to agricultural partners for rice cultivation. The agency says rice cultivation can help slow or stop subsidence while allowing the land to remain in agricultural production.Metropolitan's longer-term climate planning also identifies Webb Tract as an opportunity to test how wetland restoration and rice cultivation can reduce greenhouse gas emissions from subsided peat soils. Monitoring carried out before the project found that baseline emissions from the peat were higher than initially estimated, highlighting the potential climate benefits of changing how the land is managed.The project is not only about protecting the land from sinking. Restoring wetlands is also expected to create habitat in an area where natural wetland landscapes have been extensively altered by agriculture and other development. Keeping portions of Webb Tract wet can provide habitat for migratory birds and other Delta species. The project is being designed as a multi-benefit landscape, combining wetlands, upland habitat and rice fields rather than returning the entire island to a single land use.Wetlands can also play a role in carbon storage. Waterlogged soils can retain organic carbon that would otherwise be released as greenhouse gases when peat is drained and exposed to oxygen. Metropolitan has said the restoration could generate carbon credits because of the project's carbon-sequestration benefits. Those credits could potentially be used to offset the agency's emissions or sold in the carbon market, with revenue helping support long-term management of the restored landscape.The Webb Tract initiative has an estimated cost of about $28 million. The Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta Conservancy is providing a $20.9 million grant, while Metropolitan is funding the remainder. The project was developed with guidance from Indigenous and Delta communities, according to the announcement. The restoration is also connected to California's Cutting the Green Tape initiative, which is intended to streamline environmental review and permitting for restoration projects that provide long-term benefits for climate resilience, biodiversity and sensitive species.The official announcement says the organisations will break ground and plant the first seeds for future native plants on Oct. 7, 2026. Officials expected to participate include California Natural Resources Agency Secretary Wade Crowfoot, Metropolitan General Manager Shivaji Deshmukh, California Department of Water Resources Director Tom Gibson, California Department of Fish and Wildlife Director Meghan Hertel and Delta Conservancy Executive Officer Campbell Ingram. The first planting will include Bay Miwok evening primrose, a native plant described by the project organisers as having deep connections to the Delta's Indigenous communities.Ultimately, the Webb Tract project represents a shift from treating the Delta's subsided agricultural islands solely as farmland toward managing them as landscapes that can serve several purposes at once. By combining wetlands with rice cultivation, the project aims to keep peat soils wet, slow or reverse subsidence, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, store carbon and expand habitat while retaining an agricultural role for the island.
Article Summary: California is moving ahead with a major restoration project that will reshape about 2,800 acres of farmland on Webb Tract. The project is intended to address decades of land subsidence while reducing greenhouse gas emissions, storing carbon and creating habitat for wildlife. The approximately $28 million project is being supported by a $20.9 million grant from the Delta Conservancy.

Article Title: The US approved construction of its first commercial small modular reactor, a 300-megawatt Tennessee project that cleared a 14-month review but still needs a license before operating
Article Text:
The Clinch River project will use the BWRX-300, a boiling-water reactor developed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy

A smaller model for nuclear power

A landmark regulatory decision

Creating a template for future projects

The cost and licensing hurdles remain

The United States has taken a significant step toward a new generation of nuclear power with approval for construction of what is set to become the country’s first commercial small modular reactor (SMR). According to Reuters, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) granted the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) permission to build a 300-megawatt reactor at its Clinch River site in Roane County, Tennessee. The permit follows a 14-month technical review, but construction approval does not mean the reactor can begin producing electricity. TVA will still require a separate operating licence before fuel can be loaded and the facility brought online.Reuters reports that the Clinch River project will use the BWRX-300, a boiling-water reactor developed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy. Unlike conventional nuclear plants, which generate more than 1,000 megawatts from enormous facilities, the BWRX-300 is designed to produce up to 300 megawatts.Its smaller scale is central to the SMR concept. Modular reactors are designed so that significant sections can be manufactured in factories and transported for assembly, rather than constructing every major component at the plant site.The approach is intended to simplify construction, reduce complexity and potentially make nuclear capacity easier to add in stages as electricity demand increases, another report by Interesting Engineering states.The design also incorporates passive safety systems, which can cool the reactor using natural physical processes rather than relying continuously on operators or external power. The smaller footprint and reduced cooling-water requirements could further broaden the range of sites where such reactors can be considered, the report adds.The NRC's construction permit is only the second major advanced-reactor construction approval issued in the US and represents a milestone for TVA, which becomes the first American utility authorised to build a commercial SMR, the online report claims.The agency completed its formal technical evaluation in 14 months, a notably structured review for a new reactor design. TVA had already received an early site permit for Clinch River in 2019, giving the project a regulatory foundation before the latest construction decision. The site itself is significant. Located near Oak Ridge and the US Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Clinch River sits within one of the country's longstanding centres of nuclear research and development.The importance of the permit extends beyond Tennessee. Federal regulators and the nuclear industry view the Clinch River process as a potential model for future BWRX-300 projects in the US. A regulatory pathway established around one deployment could provide other utilities with a clearer reference point when seeking approval for similar reactors.The report also states that this could become increasingly important as utilities face growing electricity demand from data centres, artificial intelligence infrastructure and industrial activity. SMRs are being explored as a way of supplying steady electricity while incrementally adding generation capacity rather than relying exclusively on large, conventional nuclear plants.Despite the regulatory milestone, Clinch River is still some distance from operation. TVA has not announced a date for beginning construction and must secure the separate operating licence required before the reactor can be fuelled.The first commercial deployment of a new reactor design also carries financial risks. TVA is therefore pursuing cost-sharing arrangements with commercial partners, with the aim of limiting the burden on its customers while spreading the risks and benefits of the project. If the Clinch River reactor moves ahead, its significance will extend beyond its 300-megawatt output. It will serve as a real-world test of whether smaller, factory-oriented nuclear reactors can move from regulatory approval to construction and eventually provide a scalable source of round-the-clock electricity for a rapidly changing US power system.Image Courtesy: istockImage for Representation Purposes Only.
Article Summary: Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) granted permission to build a 300-megawatt reactor at its Clinch River site in Roane County, Tennessee. The reactor will use the BWRX-300, a boiling-water reactor developed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy. Unlike conventional nuclear plants, which generate more than 1,000 megawatts from enormous facilities, the reactor is designed to produce up to 300 megawatts.

Article Title: James Cagney’s former Beverly Hills estate was restored over many years, preserving its original fireplaces and leaded glass; the five-acre compound listed for $38.5 million is now asking $29.995 mill
Article Text:
James Cagney’s former estate at 9631 Cedarbrook Drive, a roughly five-acre compound tucked beneath Franklin Canyon, was once listed for $38.5 million and is now asking $29.995 million (Image Credit: Luan Pernia via Christie's)

A secluded retreat from Hollywood

Cagney established the five-acre estate in Beverly Hills in the 1930s (Image Credit: Christian Cruzio via Christie's)

Historic details were kept during the restoration

Inside, the house includes a wine cellar, kitchen, formal dining room and living areas that open towards shaded terraces (Image Credit: Christian Cruzio via Christie's)

More than just a large Beverly Hills house

A sizeable price cut

A piece of Hollywood history is back on the Beverly Hills market, but with a considerably smaller price tag. James Cagney’s former estate at 9631 Cedarbrook Drive, a roughly five-acre compound tucked beneath Franklin Canyon, was once listed for $38.5 million and is now asking $29.995 million, according to The Beverly Hills Estates. The property has also undergone years of restoration, with its original fireplaces, leaded glass and other period details carefully retained alongside modern updates. The Christie’s listing highlights how its historic character has been preserved across the sprawling compound, which once served as a private retreat for the celebrated actor.Cagney established the five-acre estate in Beverly Hills in the 1930s. The actor, who lived from 1899 to 1986, became famous for a string of memorable film roles, particularly the tough-guy characters that helped define his screen image. Away from the cameras, however, the estate offered a considerably quieter setting. Set beneath Franklin Canyon, the property has the feel of a private country retreat rather than a conventional celebrity compound. Its large grounds and natural surroundings gave Cagney a degree of separation from the city while still keeping him close to Beverly Hills.The estate has since grown into a substantial residential compound. The current listing puts the living area at about 10,778 square feet, with seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and three half-bathrooms.Much of the interest in the property comes from what has survived from its earlier years. The main villa retains exposed trussed-beam ceilings, leaded glass windows, reclaimed European terracotta roof tiles and original fireplaces that have been restored. Rather than replacing those features with an entirely contemporary interior, the restoration appears to have been approached with the property's history in mind. Christie’s describes years of work on the estate, with updated finishes incorporated alongside older architectural elements.Inside, the house includes a wine cellar, kitchen, formal dining room and living areas that open towards shaded terraces. Reclaimed 19th-century French oak is also among the materials used in the restoration, bringing another historic element into the interiors. The compound is not limited to the main residence. It includes a guest residence, a carriage house and a separate guest cottage. That cottage has an especially personal connection to Cagney because it was originally used as his art studio. Cagney’s interest in painting is another side of the actor that is often less prominent than his film career, making the preserved studio an unusual part of the property’s story.The layout of the estate is one of its defining features. Several buildings are connected by stone pathways, gardens and courtyards, creating a collection of spaces rather than making the property feel like one oversized mansion. There is also plenty built into the grounds for recreation and entertaining. The estate has a regulation tennis court, pickleball court and half basketball court, along with a swimming pool and spa. Outdoor chef’s kitchens and a poolside cabana add to the entertaining spaces.Yet it is the surrounding landscape that gives the compound much of its character. The estate is set in a canyon setting surrounded by natural landscape. At the same time, the estate remains close to the centre of Beverly Hills. Landscaping adds another layer of privacy, with mature greenery surrounding the buildings and a large banyan tree positioned near the motor court.The property's price history changed notably in 2026. It was listed for $38.5 million on February 6 before being withdrawn on June 11. A new listing went live on June 12 with an asking price of $29.995 million. The reduction puts the estate back on the market at a price nearly $8.5 million below its earlier asking figure.But the property is being presented as more than a luxury home with a long list of amenities. Its connection to Cagney, the age of the main residence and the restoration of its period features give it a story that a newly constructed mansion cannot easily replicate. Nearly a century after Cagney made the estate his home, the compound still combines the privacy of a large hillside property with access to Beverly Hills. Its restored fireplaces, leaded glass, old timber and former art studio offer reminders of the people and period that shaped the estate, while the newer amenities make the sprawling property suited to contemporary use.
Article Summary: Cagney established the five-acre estate in Beverly Hills in the 1930s. The property has undergone years of restoration, with its original fireplaces, leaded glass and other period details carefully retained. The current listing puts the living area at about 10,778 square feet, with seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and three half-bathrooms.

Article Title: In 2021, a California couple bought a home and faced more than $1 million in fines linked to the previous owner's cannabis operation; five years later, a settlement cleared the disputed penalties
Article Text:
cannabisRepresentative image

A home purchase followed by a huge bill

Representative image

How the county’s fine system worked

A wider group of affected owners

The legal battle lasted four years

What the settlement changes

Why the case matters to homeowners

A new chapter for the property owners

When Corrine and Doug Thomas bought a property in Humboldt County, California, in 2021, they expected to take ownership of a home and land. Instead, they inherited a legal dispute connected to the previous owner’s alleged cannabis operation. County officials sought more than $1 million in penalties against the couple, along with roughly $200,000 to demolish a barn where cannabis had reportedly been grown. Five years later, a settlement has withdrawn the disputed notices, fines and fees. The Institute for Justice said the agreement also requires Humboldt County to reform its code enforcement process. Court records available through Justia show that the case challenged how the county imposed cannabis-related penalties on property owners who disputed the alleged violations.The Thomases’ ordeal began after they purchased the property in 2021. According to the Institute for Justice, Humboldt County treated conditions linked to the previous owner’s cannabis activity as violations that continued to affect the property after the sale. The couple said they had not committed the alleged violations and were not responsible for the earlier operation. Yet the county pursued penalties against them based on the property’s history and the structures located on the land.The financial exposure grew quickly. The Thomases faced more than $1 million in civil penalties, as well as an estimated $200,000 cost to demolish a barn behind the home. For a newly arrived property owner, the potential liability was far greater than an ordinary code violation fine.The case raised a basic question about property ownership. Should a buyer be held financially responsible for alleged activity conducted by someone else before the buyer acquired the land?Humboldt County’s cannabis code enforcement system allowed penalties to accumulate on a daily basis. According to reports about the lawsuit, fines could reach $10,000 or $12,000 per day, depending on the violation and the applicable county rules.The Institute for Justice argued that the system effectively placed the burden on property owners to prove their innocence. Attorneys said county officials used satellite images and other indicators to identify suspected unpermitted cannabis activity, sometimes without fully investigating who had carried out the work or when it had occurred. Once a violation notice was issued, the penalties could continue while the owner waited for a hearing. That created a serious financial problem for people who wanted to challenge the allegations, because the amount at stake could grow dramatically before they had an opportunity to present evidence.For the Thomases, the county’s position meant that buying the property had not ended the previous owner’s alleged legal problems. Instead, the consequences followed the land and became the new owners’ responsibility to contest.The Thomases were not the only property owners involved in the lawsuit. The Institute for Justice represented five people who challenged Humboldt County’s enforcement practices. Another plaintiff, Rhonda Olson, reportedly faced proposed penalties totalling millions of dollars on properties she purchased after earlier cannabis activity had ended.The case also involved property owners who said they were accused of violations they did not commit, as per reports. One plaintiff, Blu Graham, waited years for a hearing to show that a greenhouse on his property was being used for vegetables rather than cannabis, according to reporting about the case. The different circumstances shared a common concern. The owners said county officials treated satellite images, property features or past activity as sufficient evidence of violations, while failing to provide a prompt process for correcting mistakes.The lawsuit argued that excessive fines and delayed hearings violated constitutional protections, including the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on excessive fines and due process guarantees.The property owners filed the federal lawsuit in 2022. The litigation continued as the plaintiffs challenged the county’s enforcement framework and the way penalties were imposed. The case did not immediately end when the property owners asked courts to intervene. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a petition concerning whether the plaintiffs were entitled to a jury trial in the proceedings.However, the lawsuit continued in the federal courts. The Ninth Circuit allowed claims concerning excessive fines to move forward after finding that the property owners had plausibly alleged that the county’s practices violated constitutional protections.That ruling increased pressure on the county to resolve the dispute. Rather than continue through a full trial, Humboldt County entered into a settlement with the plaintiffs.Under the agreement, Humboldt County will withdraw all outstanding cannabis-related notices of violation, fines and fees challenged by the five property owners. That means the Thomases will no longer face the more than $1 million in penalties linked to the property. The county also agreed to pay $350,000 towards the plaintiffs’ expenses and attorneys’ fees. The payment is not described as an admission of wrongdoing by the county. The settlement requires several changes to the enforcement process. Before imposing future cannabis-related penalties, the county must provide property owners with a warning and 30 days to respond. Owners will also be entitled to a hearing within 60 days. Fines will not continue accumulating while the hearing process is pending, addressing one of the central concerns raised by the plaintiffs. The federal court will retain jurisdiction over the settlement for three years. That gives the court authority to address disputes over whether the county follows the agreed reforms.The case shows how property-related penalties can create serious risks for buyers. A homeowner may purchase land without knowing that a prior owner’s activities could later trigger fines, demolition demands or legal action.It also highlights the importance of due process in local code enforcement. Governments have authority to regulate buildings, land use and cannabis cultivation, but property owners need a meaningful opportunity to understand allegations and challenge them before penalties become overwhelming. The settlement does not prevent Humboldt County from enforcing its cannabis rules. Instead, it changes when and how the county can impose penalties, requiring advance notice and a timely hearing.For the Thomases, the agreement brings an end to a financial threat connected to a property they did not own when the alleged cannabis activity occurred. For other homeowners, the reforms may prevent a similar situation from lasting for years.The settlement clears the disputed penalties and removes the immediate threat of a million-dollar bill from the Thomases’ home. It also ends a legal struggle that began soon after they purchased the property and continued for roughly four years. The broader lesson is that code enforcement can affect more than the person accused of violating a rule. When fines attach to land, later buyers can become involved even if they had no role in the conduct that prompted the penalties.Humboldt County’s revised process now requires the government to communicate with owners before issuing fines and to provide a prompt forum for disputes. Whether those reforms work as intended will be monitored over the next three years.For Corrine and Doug Thomas, however, the immediate outcome is clear. The penalties tied to the former owner’s alleged cannabis operation have been withdrawn, allowing the couple to keep their home without carrying a financial burden created before they ever bought it.
Article Summary: Corrine and Doug Thomas bought a property in Humboldt County, California, in 2021. They inherited a legal dispute connected to the previous owner’s alleged cannabis operation. County officials sought more than $1 million in penalties against the couple, along with roughly $200,000 to demolish a barn where cannabis had reportedly been grown. Five years later, a settlement has withdrawn the disputed notices, fines and fees.

Article Title: New Zealand built a 676-square-metre pest-proof sanctuary for rare skinks; four were released in 2026 to rebuild a mainland population
Article Text:
Northern spotted skink (Oligosoma kokowai) in Napier. Image credit: Nick Harker/ New Zealand Herpetological Society

How the new 676-square-metre sanctuary protects the skinks

Napier spotted skink sanctuary habitat. Image credit: Nick Harker/New Zealand Herpetological Society

Survival challenges for the northern spotted skinks

Importance of first 4 releases for the skink population

How stormwater work shaped the relocation of skinks

What comes next for the rare skinks

New Zealand has created a 676-square-metre pest-proof sanctuary in Napier for the northern spotted skink, a rare native reptile whose Hawke’s Bay population is considered critically endangered. The purpose-built enclosure was completed in late 2025, and on 18 April 2026, four skinks were released into their new home. The move is intended to protect the remaining population while creating a safer place where the species can survive and potentially breed. The sanctuary also forms part of a wider effort to protect the skinks as major stormwater improvements are carried out nearby. The New Zealand Herpetological Society reported these details.The sanctuary was built on a foreshore reserve that had previously been mown grass, so its habitat had to be created rather than simply protected. The New Zealand Herpetological Society says the site now includes deep rock piles, large logs, driftwood and plants that can provide food and shelter.Napier City Council describes the enclosure as a 26-metre by 26-metre space on Marine Parade. Its 2-metre-high fence uses fine mesh to keep out predators, including mice, rats and cats.A cap at the top of the fence makes it harder for climbing or jumping animals to get inside.The council says the enclosure also includes basking areas, rock and wood piles, vegetation and small edible fruits for the skinks. Entry is restricted to approved personnel so the habitat can be maintained and monitored.The design was developed with herpetologists and conservation specialists, according to Napier City Council. The National Aquarium of New Zealand, Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, Biodiversity Hawke’s Bay, mana whenua, community groups and local schools have also been involved.The northern spotted skink, scientifically known as Oligosoma kokowai, has become extremely rare across New Zealand. According to the New Zealand Herpetological Society, the species is regionally critically endangered in Hawke’s Bay and survives at only one location in Napier. The local animals are also genetically distinct from northern spotted skinks found further south, making this population particularly important.The species once lived across parts of the upper South Island and lower North Island. The New Zealand Herpetological Society says habitat destruction and introduced predators such as rats, mice and cats have pushed the skinks towards extinction in the North Island. Today, they survive on 3 pest-free islands in the Wellington region and in 3 small mainland populations.Napier’s skinks have faced their own long decline. They once lived among coastal plants such as Muehlenbeckia, but much of that habitat was cleared and replaced with mown lawn during the 1960s and 1970s. The population was thought to have disappeared until a small group was rediscovered in 2006.The first release took place on 18 April 2026, when two males and two females were placed inside the sanctuary. The New Zealand Herpetological Society reported that each skink had been photographed before release because its individual markings can be used to identify it later.That means future surveys can show whether the original four animals remain in the enclosure and whether any young are born there. The skinks will continue to be monitored for survival and breeding.The release is only an early step. The New Zealand Herpetological Society says the sanctuary could eventually hold up to 300 northern spotted skinks, but reaching anything close to that number is expected to take many years because so few animals remain and the species breeds slowly.The conservation group also hopes that more northern spotted skinks can be found and moved into the sanctuary. Bringing in additional animals could increase the genetic diversity of the small population.The sanctuary was created alongside a major stormwater project between Maraenui and Te Awa. Napier City Council says the enclosure was built as mitigation because the infrastructure upgrades would affect skink habitat.RNZ’s Local Democracy Reporting, in its January 2026 report, said the skinks were being moved to make way for a $37.4 million stormwater infrastructure project. The work includes a new pump station, a coastal outfall on Marine Parade and upgrades to watercourses, with construction planned to improve Napier’s flood resilience.The council considered the enclosure a way to allow the infrastructure work to continue while providing permanent protection for the skinks. RNZ reported that the project site was considered the most cost-effective location for the stormwater outfall.The sanctuary therefore serves two purposes at once. It provides a protected home for an endangered local reptile while allowing important infrastructure work to proceed.The immediate priority is to keep the new enclosure free of predators and closely follow what happens to the 4 founding skinks. The New Zealand Herpetological Society says ongoing surveillance will be needed to ensure the sanctuary remains pest-free.For a population that may once have numbered fewer than 25 animals, the release represents a significant conservation step. The organisation said surveys in the early 2020s indicated that the Napier population was at high risk of extinction without intervention.
Article Summary: New Zealand has created a 676-square-metre sanctuary in Napier for the northern spotted skink. The species is regionally critically endangered in Hawke’s Bay and survives at only one location. The sanctuary was built on a foreshore reserve that had previously been mown grass, so its habitat had to be created. The New Zealand Herpetological Society says the site now includes deep rock piles, large logs, driftwood and plants.

Article Title: A wildlife charity bought 335 hectares in Dorset; two years later, it is one of England’s newest National Nature Reserves
Article Text:
Representative Image of a vibrant landscape of chalk grassland and wildflower meadows at Lyscombe National Nature Reserve (AI Generated Image)

From farmland to National Nature Reserve

Restoring the chalk grassland and Little Piddle

Monitoring a landscape in transition

A long-term project beyond the reserve

In March 2024, Dorset Wildlife Trust and Natural England acquired 335 hectares of chalk downland and farmland at Lyscombe, around 10 miles north-east of Dorchester. The former organically managed farm was acquired for nature conservation and environmental restoration, with funding from Natural England’s National Nature Reserves programme and its planned nutrient mitigation credit scheme, alongside donations from Dorset Wildlife Trust members and supporters. In 2026, Lyscombe became the 16th site in the King’s Series of National Nature Reserves. Natural England formally declared the reserve on 17 August, while its new status was publicly announced and celebrated on 15 September. The formal declaration covers 333.57 hectares, while Dorset Wildlife Trust describes the original acquisition as 335 hectares. The landscape includes chalk grassland, wildflower meadows, scrub, ancient woodland and historic features, with restoration work focused on restoring habitats and creating better-connected spaces for wildlife.The new status was celebrated at Lyscombe on 15 September, when Jaqueline Swift, Deputy Lord-Lieutenant of Dorset, represented His Majesty the King at an event attended by Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, and Lisbet Sherlock, Chair of Dorset Wildlife Trust. Swift and Juniper unveiled the National Nature Reserve plaque, while Juniper presented Sherlock and Dorset Wildlife Trust chief executive Brian Bleese with the certificate recognising Lyscombe’s new status.The legal declaration had been made on 17 August 2026 under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. The reserve includes 50 hectares of nationally important chalk downland designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, as well as a Site of Nature Conservation Interest and several protected heritage features. Among them is Lyscombe Chapel, a Grade II* listed building that dates from the 12th century but was partly rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries. Historic England records substantial medieval fabric, including a 12th-century chancel. The nearby ruins of the Priest’s House date from the 16th century.The conservation work began before the National Nature Reserve designation. Dorset Wildlife Trust says it has removed up to 23 kilometres of outdated fencing and introduced English Longhorn cattle onto the SSSI chalk grassland. The grazing is intended to maintain the open character of the chalk grassland, prevent scrub encroachment and support biodiversity. The Trust is also pursuing restoration of the Little Piddle, which rises at Lyscombe and is a tributary of the River Piddle. Its plans include returning the stream towards a more natural course, removing concrete culverts and outdated agricultural infrastructure, and creating wetland habitat and fen meadows in the valley bottom. Dorset Wildlife Trust says that changing land management and creating new wetland habitat at Lyscombe will help reduce harmful nutrient inputs into the Poole Harbour catchment, while Natural England says the project has contributed to reducing historic pollution in the local River Piddle. The acquisition was also partly funded through Natural England’s nutrient mitigation scheme, linking the land purchase to wider efforts to reduce nutrient pollution in the Poole Harbour catchment.Dorset Wildlife Trust is carrying out ecological, soil and hydrological surveys to establish baselines and guide future management, with monitoring covering invertebrates, small mammals, bats, breeding birds and flora. In 2025, the Trust worked with the Environmental Sensing department at the University of Southampton to enable a student to create a virtual tour of Lyscombe using ArcGIS StoryMaps. The project incorporated drone data collected at the site and included a 3D model of the landscape. The Trust also reports that barn owls have returned since the acquisition, which it links to a resurgence of small mammals in the fields and hedgerows. That is an observation reported by the Trust rather than an independent assessment of the cause. Alongside the ecological work, Dorset Wildlife Trust is working with Historic England on heritage features including the chapel and the ruined Priest’s House, while also planning restoration of existing barns. The project therefore combines habitat restoration and wildlife monitoring with the protection of a landscape containing significant archaeological and historic features.Lyscombe’s National Nature Reserve designation gives national recognition to a project that began with the 2024 acquisition, but the restoration itself is intended to continue for years. Natural England describes the reserve as 334 hectares and says it has potential to contribute to nature recovery across the wider 5,700-hectare Dorset Downs landscape. Dorset Wildlife Trust’s plans combine conservation management of the existing SSSI with natural regeneration and a rewilding approach across wider parts of the site. The Trust says the land is likely to develop into a mosaic of grassland, scrub and wood pasture, supported by appropriate grazing and natural regeneration. Lyscombe already supports at least six orchid species, including pyramidal and bee orchids, as well as chalkhill blue butterflies and other wildlife. The reserve’s new status does not mark the completion of that work. Instead, it formally recognises the national importance of the landscape while Dorset Wildlife Trust continues its longer-term programme of habitat restoration, ecological monitoring, conservation grazing and work to reconnect Lyscombe with the wider Dorset Downs.
Article Summary: In 2024, Dorset Wildlife Trust and Natural England acquired 335 hectares of chalk downland and farmland at Lyscombe, around 10 miles north-east of Dorchester. The former organically managed farm was acquired for nature conservation and environmental restoration. In 2026, Lyscombe became the 16th site in the King’s Series of National Nature Reserves.

NEW DELHI: The Indian Coast Guard , in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), seized approximately 526 kg of narcotics from an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The Coast Guard said five Pakistani nationals operating the vessel were also detained during the operation carried out near Lakshadweep on September 25, as reported by news agency PTI.The drugs, valued at over Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, were seized after the vessel was intercepted during the operation.The Coast Guard conducted coordinated sea-air surveillance to track the suspicious vessel before launching a hot pursuit and boarding the dhow.The operation was carried out in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) to intercept the vessel. Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Student protests rock France with over 400 detained: Why are schools protesting - explained
Article Text:
File photo: A student walks past a burning bicycle next to the Baggio High School, blocked in protest of the government's release of next year's draft budget, in Lille, France

Students take protests beyond Paris

Civil servants join nationwide strike

Why the budget is at the centre of the anger

Poll Vote & Share your view Which area should receive greater priority in France’s upcoming budget? Education Healthcare Public Safety Infrastructure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

France was hit by a nationwide wave of strikes and student protests, with civil servants walking off the job and high school students blocking hundreds of schools as anger over budget cuts, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages spread across the country.The mobilisation came two days before Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government is due to present its draft 2027 budget, which includes a planned €54 billion savings drive. The protests have added to pressure on the government as it tries to rein in France's finances ahead of next year's presidential election.The unrest was particularly visible at schools, where students piled up bins and barriers to prevent access. The education ministry said around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday, out of roughly 3,700 nationwide. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, according to interior minister Laurent Nuñez.​​At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured during Tuesday's unrest, according to officials.The school protests began in the Paris region last week but have since spread to cities including Lille, Lyon, Nantes, Marseille, Bordeaux and Rennes.Students have been protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, poor school conditions and demanding timetables. At some schools, however, the demonstrations escalated into clashes with police.In Lille, rubbish bins were set on fire outside the Lycée César Baggio, while police used tear gas and batons after protesters threw objects. Similar confrontations were reported elsewhere, although many blockades remained peaceful.At the Lycée Arago in Paris, students blocked the entrance with bins while a placard reading "Macron explosion" was displayed. Outside the Hélène-Boucher school, protesters put up a banner saying "Fewer cops, More money"."We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally," final-year student Mael Breton told Reuters.Students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions as key grievances. “There are 34 of us in each class, and it’s just not feasible. The teachers are overworked,” a 16-year-old student told AFP, saying the education system was “completely broken.”The government's response has been mixed. Lecornu condemned violence around schools but acknowledged that students' concerns over the education system needed to be heard and addressed. Education minister Édouard Geffray said students had a right to protest but condemned violence as "indefensible".The student mobilisation coincided with a broader strike by public-sector workers, including teachers, healthcare workers and firefighters.Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France to oppose the government's budget plans and its proposed freeze on state employees' base salaries in 2027. The CGT union has argued that repeated pay freezes have eroded workers' purchasing power.Firefighters were among those taking part after a summer of major wildfires exposed concerns over resources. The education ministry said just over 11% of teachers and other school staff were on strike, while participation among other civil servants was below 10%.Transport disruption was limited in the morning, although the aviation regulator warned of possible disruption at some airports.CGT leader Sophie Binet said the government had 48 hours to reverse the planned spending cuts before the union considers further strike action."This summer, who was on the front line? It wasn't the billionaires, the big bosses or the shareholders. It was civil servants and working people. And how are they being thanked? By cutting their pay? The anger is enormous," she told BFMTV.Lecornu's government is trying to find savings as France grapples with a mounting debt burden. The proposed €54 billion savings package is aimed at bringing the public deficit down, while the government has also warned that public debt could reach 121.7% of GDP in 2027.France's public debt reached €3.595 trillion at the end of June, or around 119% of GDP, according to national statistics agency Insee.The cost of servicing that debt is also rising. France is expected to spend around €79 billion on interest payments this year, with the government projecting the figure could rise to €91 billion in 2027.The government is therefore trying to cut spending while unions resist pay restraint and students demand more teachers and resources for schools.
Article Summary: Around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, interior minister says. At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured. Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France.

Article Title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
Article Text:
The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections

‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US voters

‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulers

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that Iran's appeal to American voters will influence the outcome of the midterm elections? Yes, it will have a significant impact No, it will not influence the elections Possibly, but only to a limited extent 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.The letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material.The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. The currency has repeatedly hit new lows since the war began.
Article Summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: In 2014, a woman left Oregon alone to walk the world; after six and a half years, she returned with 20,000 miles and one terrifying attack behind her
Article Text:
Angela Maxwell set out on an extraordinary six and a half year quest to walk around the globe, departing from Bend, Oregon. Image Credits: Instagram @Angela Maxwell

A journey planned one leg at a time

The night in Mongolia

Despite facing adversities like a harrowing assault in Mongolia, Maxwell persevered, fostering connections with people she met. Upon her return to Bend, her journey culminated in profound reflections on simplicity and transformation. Image Credits: Instagram@ Angela Maxwell

Six and a half years later

On 2 May 2014, Angela Maxwell left Bend, Oregon, with a two-wheeled cart, camping equipment and no fixed end date. She had decided to walk around the world, despite having little previous experience with long-distance hiking. What began as an unusual personal challenge eventually became a six-and-a-half-year journey across four continents, 14 countries and more than 20,000 miles.According to ABC News, Maxwell had been working as a life coach and business consultant when she began thinking about making a major change. She had heard about people who had travelled around the world on foot and became fascinated by the idea. Within about nine months, she had sold most of her belongings, prepared her equipment and set off. Her journey was not a continuous walk the entire way. She used flights between some destinations and walked for long stretches once she arrived.Maxwell's preparation was relatively short for an expedition of such scale. She told ABC that she had no previous hiking experience and spent about nine months researching equipment, reading about women adventurers and building up her fitness.She eventually carried her belongings in a two-wheeled cart, which became a familiar part of her journey. She spent about $5 a day, which meant camping much of the time and carrying her own food and water. Her meals were often simple, including oatmeal and instant noodles. The cart held her tent, cooking equipment, clothing and other supplies, allowing her to remain largely self-sufficient while travelling.Her route changed as she travelled. She walked from Bend to Portland, then flew to Western Australia and travelled north through some of the country's harshest terrain. She later continued through New Zealand, Southeast Asia, Mongolia and Europe. Her route later took her through Italy, Georgia, Turkey, Switzerland, France, Belgium, England and Scotland before she returned to the United States. The physical demands were considerable. In Australia, she experienced heat stroke and severe sun blisters. In Vietnam, she contracted dengue fever and spent about a month recovering. Yet Maxwell has said that the walking itself was not always the hardest part. Being alone and deciding whether it was safe to continue often required more from her than the distance did.According to BBC Travel, about a year into her journey, Maxwell experienced one of its most frightening moments in Mongolia when a nomad broke into her tent and sexually assaulted her. After the attack, she moved away from the campsite and spent the remaining hours of darkness hiding with her cart before deciding what to do next. Despite the experience, Maxwell continued her journey and eventually completed her walk around the world.It was the only time during the expedition when she seriously thought about giving up on the trip. Maxwell went on to say that thinking about stories of other women who had managed to survive an attack inspired her to keep going. This experience made her rethink how she approached her safety. Throughout the rest of the trip, she was more vigilant at night, especially when camping out, and she took further steps to protect herself in her tent. She chose to include this experience in her story, but it did not define the entire trip. Most of Maxwell's experiences were with people who helped her on her journey.Maxwell reached her destination on December 16, 2020, and returned to Bend, where her journey had begun, to the home of the friend who had helped her set out on the adventure. By then, she had covered more than 20,000 miles and spent six and a half years travelling from one country to another and from one landscape to another. Finishing the trip was not easy. Later, Maxwell said she had changed after years without belongings, talking to strangers and living with uncertainty. When she returned, walking had taken on a different meaning: an attempt to lead a life based on simplicity, travelling slowly and figuring out how far she could go on her own.
Article Summary: Angela Maxwell set out on a six-and-a-half-year quest to walk around the globe. She left Bend, Oregon, on 2 May 2014 with a two-wheeled cart, camping equipment and no fixed end date. Her route took her through four continents, 14 countries and more than 20,000 miles.

Article Title: After Utah removed invasive brown trout from a mountain stream for 4 years, native Bonneville cutthroat trout recovered to near-carrying capacity within 6 years
Article Text:
After nearly eight years, a project started in 2008 by BLM-Utah, Utah-DWR and Trout Unlimited to continues to successfully increase native fish populations in northern Utah. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Removing the fish that had taken over

Native trout get another chance

The restoration removed a competing non-native population and then allowed the native fish to establish themselves in habitat that had previously been occupied by brown trout. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

What the recovery tells researchers

Removing an established fish population from a mountain stream is not a simple task. Even after the unwanted fish are gone, there is no guarantee that native species will return in large numbers. In a tributary of Utah's Logan River, however, researchers found that native Bonneville cutthroat trout could recover surprisingly quickly after non-native brown trout were removed.According to the US Geological Survey (USGS) , the long-running experiment took place in Right Hand Fork, a tributary where non-native brown trout had become established alongside the native Bonneville cutthroat trout. Researchers had monitored the fish community for a decade before beginning the removal programme. The four-year effort included two years of mechanical removal followed by two years of chemical treatment. After the brown trout were eradicated, the researchers introduced relatively small numbers of cutthroat trout eggs and young fish. Within six years of the eradication, the native population had recovered to close to the stream's estimated carrying capacity.According to Conservation Science and Practice , the Right Hand Fork is part of the Logan River watershed in northern Utah and provides habitat for Bonneville cutthroat trout.Brown trout had become established in the tributary by the late 1990s, and before the restoration work, the stream was dominated by the non-native species rather than supporting a resident population of cutthroat trout. Researchers identified competition from brown trout as one of the pressures affecting native cutthroat trout in the wider Logan River system. The researchers first spent 10 years collecting information on the stream's fish populations. This gave them a baseline against which they could measure what happened after the brown trout were removed.The first step involved the use of mechanical removal techniques such as electro-fishing. After this came the second stage, which involved two years of chemical application, aiming at eliminating all the brown trout. This four-year process was not simply one of removing all the fish once and then letting the stream take care of itself. It took repeated efforts since brown trout would live or come back to a part of a stream system. Past experience in the Logan River had proved how hard it was to get rid of brown trout. Through two years of mechanical removal, 15,000 brown trout were removed from 5.6 kilometers of Right Hand Fork.After the removal of brown trout from the ecosystem, however, the scientists did not leave the recovery process to chance. They introduced a small number of eggs and young fish of cutthroat trout into the ecosystem. In this way, the experiment evaluated the influence of both factors – elimination of the competitor and the introduction of a new source population for the native fish. Results came fast. Scientists calculated the growth rate and the carrying capacity of the population based on monitoring results during several years. After six years of eradication and seeding of brown trout population reached the carrying capacity of the stream. At least four age classes existed, including adult fish suitable for anglers.The recovery was also consistent with earlier research showing that brown trout can affect the performance of native Bonneville cutthroat trout. A field experiment published in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society examined brown trout's effects on native cutthroat trout at both individual and population levels, providing evidence that interactions between the two species can influence the native fish population. The result was therefore not simply a case of fish numbers rising after a stocking exercise. The restoration removed a competing non-native population and then allowed the native fish to establish themselves in habitat that had previously been occupied by brown trout.The modelling of the cutthroat population by the researchers gave an optimistic long-term outlook. This is because the model showed that there was a 95% chance that the cutthroat trout population would have attained at least 90% of its carrying capacity after 10 years of brown trout eradication. This does not mean all the streams will show a similar trend. The study location had healthy habitat, and the researchers stated that removal of invader species could be influenced by the size and status of the ecosystem, among other factors.However, they also noted that such small tributaries as the Right Hand Fork were constrained by size. Any larger benefits might result from their ability to serve as source populations that enable native trout to thrive in the downstream reaches of a river system. The research provided an informative illustration of how the native fish might fare in conditions when they have the opportunity for restoration. Four years of brown trout elimination and six years of monitoring resulted in the population of Bonneville cutthroat trout being on par with the maximum capacity of the stream to support them. The restoration did not take several decades but was fast.
Article Summary: The restoration removed a competing non-native population and then allowed the native fish to establish themselves in habitat that had previously been occupied by brown trout. After six years of eradication and seeding of brown trout population reached the carrying capacity of the stream. At least four age classes existed, including adult fish suitable for anglers.

Article Title: Nashville replaced 6.5 acres of parking with Cumberland Park; a hidden tank beneath it now captures about 1 million gallons of stormwater from nearby streets each year
Article Text:
The visitors center at the Cumberland Gap National Historical Park. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

From parking lot to public park

Water hidden beneath the landscape

Cumberland Park, opened in 2012 in Nashville, transformed a former parking area into a public park. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A park with several jobs

A large paved parking area is not usually thought of as part of a city's water infrastructure. In Nashville, Tennessee, however, a former parking site along the Cumberland River was transformed into Cumberland Park, a 6.5-acre public space designed to combine recreation with measures for managing rainwater.According to City Parks Alliance , Cumberland Park opened in 2012 as part of Nashville's wider riverfront redevelopment. Beneath the landscaped park is a rainwater-harvesting cistern that captures stormwater from the park, nearby streets and parking areas. The system can collect about 1 million gallons of water in a typical year, which is then reused to irrigate the park.Cumberland Park sits on the east bank of the Cumberland River, beneath the Shelby Street Bridge, on a 6.5-acre site that was once largely occupied by surface parking and other developed land. The redevelopment turned the area into a public landscape with lawns, walking paths, play areas, gardens, a climbing wall and an outdoor amphitheatre. The project formed part of Nashville's New Riverfront Revitalisation Plan, which aimed to reconnect downtown with the river, while its design also had to account for the area's floodplain. The 2010 Nashville floods, when the Cumberland River reached levels not seen since the 1930s, led designers to reconsider parts of the project before construction was completed. According to the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation , the redevelopment also included brownfield remediation, floodplain preservation and habitat restoration, with more than 1.6 acres of meadow and riparian grasses restored as part of the project.Among other features of Cumberland Park is the stormwater management system. According to the City Parks Alliance, there is also an underground cistern which is able to collect around 1 million gallons of stormwater annually. In addition, this water is not discharged to the municipal stormwater system but is used for irrigation purposes. Initially, the design of the project explained the system of collecting the stormwater from the park, as well as the parking lot and adjacent vehicle bridge.This is one instance where a city park does more than just offer empty spaces. In this park, rainwater is not drained away but instead stored in the ground and then used at a later time. This is especially significant in a place like Nashville, where heavy rainfall leads to large amounts of surface runoff. In this city, the stormwater system typically moves rainwater through the drains, pipes and ditches into creeks and rivers. The runoff from the streets might even have pollutants mixed in.Managing stormwater runoff was only a portion of the redevelopment of Cumberland Park. It was also hoped that Cumberland Park would provide new green space along a portion of the riverfront area where there was previously a predominance of paving and industry. There is an amphitheatre at Cumberland Park that can hold up to 1,200 individuals, as well as water-play elements, paths, and areas for recreation. In addition, native and traditional planting was included in the landscaping of the site, and meadow and riparian restoration added plants to the riverfront area.Contaminants found during the assessment process included Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons, Lead, and Arsenic in various sections of the former brownfield. It included processes such as soil excavation, capping of certain sites and institutional controls before the land could be put back into use as a public park. Therefore, the water collection process is part of a bigger redevelopment project. The former parking lot has been transformed to become public space, the contaminated land has been remediated, vegetation planted, and rainwater harvested.The Cumberland Park project demonstrates how one piece of urban land can be used in more than one way. On the surface level, the park is an area where people can walk, play, and meet by the river. Beneath the surface, the infrastructure is able to store rainwater. Once impervious and paved, the land has been redeveloped to catch and reuse some of the rainwater.
Article Summary: Cumberland Park, opened in 2012 in Nashville, Tennessee, transformed a former parking area into a public park. Beneath the landscaped park is a rainwater- harvesting cistern that captures stormwater from the park, nearby streets and parking areas. The system can collect about 1 million gallons of water in a typical year, which is then reused to irrigate the park.

Article Title: In 2019, Los Angeles tested a road mix made from old asphalt and recycled plastic bottles, aiming to repave streets without adding new asphalt
Article Text:
Representative image of workers using recycled plastic and old asphalt in a road-paving project. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Turning old asphalt and bottles into a new road

A pilot designed to cut out new material

In a groundbreaking initiative, Los Angeles has launched a pilot program to recycle used asphalt through a synthetic binder derived from reclaimed plastic bottles. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Testing plastic roads in the real world

A road rebuilt largely from the material already beneath it sounds straightforward, but conventional resurfacing often involves removing old material, hauling it away and bringing in fresh asphalt. According to Fast Company, in 2019, Los Angeles began testing a different approach: grind up the existing road, add a synthetic binder made partly from recycled plastic bottles and lay the material back down.The pilot was based on a simple idea. Instead of treating the old road as waste and relying on new petroleum-based bitumen to bind recycled pavement, the existing asphalt could be processed in place and held together with a binder derived from recycled polyethene terephthalate, or PET. The proposed system therefore combined two waste materials, old pavement and discarded plastic bottles, in one road-recycling process.This approach, which was developed by TechniSoil Industrial, involved the use of what the company referred to as a continuous recycling train. First, the equipment mills the surface of the old road and crushes the asphalt to the required size.It was then mixed with a liquid synthetic binder, which had been produced using recycled PET and laid down on the road again. This method differs from conventional resurfacing because the top layer of the old road can be recycled without being removed and replaced with new hot-mix asphalt.According to Construction and Building Materials , research on plastic-modified asphalt has found that the behaviour of the finished pavement depends on factors such as the type of plastic, the amount used and the way it is incorporated. PET is among the plastics investigated for improving properties such as stability, although researchers also note that high plastic contents can affect other characteristics of an asphalt mixture. The Los Angeles experiment was therefore not simply a matter of mixing shredded bottles into ordinary asphalt. The plastic was processed into a synthetic binder that served a different function in the road material.The system’s appeal was that it could reduce the amount of material moved for road construction. With the traditional method, crews would have to mill and haul away the pavement, then bring new material to the construction site. This system was designed to carry out those steps continuously on site. Fast Company also noted that in October 2019, the city of Los Angeles wanted to conduct tests on two different areas of road in December. The duration of the trial run would be one to two years.The environmental benefit also depended on the process temperature. Unlike traditional hot-mix asphalt paving, the technology worked at normal temperatures and avoided transporting both the old material and the replacement material. The company projected that the process would greatly reduce emissions, but these figures were estimates rather than measurements from the completed roadway. Los Angeles had also been increasing its use of reclaimed asphalt pavement, with Asphalt Plant No. 1 expected to raise the share of recycled asphalt pavement in its hot-mix asphalt from 20% to 50%. This broader effort provided context for the trial, as the city was exploring ways to keep more pavement material in use rather than sending it to waste.The idea attracted attention partly because the company said laboratory tests suggest plastic-based roads could last eight to 13 times longer than conventional asphalt. Research published in the Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering similarly shows that recycled plastics can influence asphalt's mechanical and thermal properties, but stresses that compatibility, storage stability, processing methods and long-term performance remain important considerations.This trial mattered because it was a real-world application, though it did not prove that plastic roads could replace conventional roads everywhere. It aimed to combine recycled PET and asphalt in a way that reduced the amount of binder needed and cut transportation of materials. It also suggested a model in which road repairs become a recycling process, with the old road forming much of the new one.
