Article Summary: Los Angeles has launched a pilot program to recycle used asphalt through a synthetic binder derived from reclaimed plastic bottles. The pilot was based on a simple idea. Instead of treating the old road as waste and relying on new petroleum-based bitumen to bind recycled pavement, the existing asphalt could be processed in place and held together with a binder. The company projected that the process would greatly reduce emissions.

Article Title: In 2020, researchers compressed sand with only about 10% polyethylene; their structural material achieved flexural strength comparable to typical steel-reinforced concrete in tests
Article Text:
Representative image of testing machine pressing down hard on a solid rectangular block made of a grey sand-composite structural material. (Image Credits: Perplexity.ai)

“Sand-Filler Structural Material with Low Content of

Polyethylene Binder

,”

How the sand-polyethylene material was made

Representative image of concrete material made from compressed sand and plastic. (Image Credits: Chatgpt)

The materials’ performance was determined by heating and processing

Researchers in 2020 developed a structural material through the combination of sand with only about 10 wt% polyethylene and compacting the mixture under pressure. The study published as showed by using about 10 wt% polyethylene and 70–100 MPa of compaction pressure, the formulation produced flexural strength greater than typical steel-reinforced concrete.In lieu of using Portland cement, polyethylene, a common plastic, was used to bind sand particles together. The idea behind this approach was to reduce the amount of polymer normally required in constructing plastic based materials and to determine if it was possible to create a different route for recycling waste plastics. The polyethylene particles used were around 40-50 micrometers in size and sand which met the required ASTM C33/33M. The binder content was varied from 4 wt% to 30 wt%, while compaction pressure ranged from 70 MPa to 350 MPa.The sand and polyethylene (PE) particles were manually mixed before being placed in a steel mold heated at about 200°C, it was then subjected to compaction pressures ranging from 70 to 350 MPa. To distribute the binder, researchers weren’t reliant on extensive mechanical mixing which made the process different from when using conventional polymer cement.Under pressure, the sand grains started to shift, rotate, deform slightly, and drove the melted polyethylene towards the contact points between neighboring grains.Following this arrangement allowed a small amount to contribute largely to the strength of the material. Researchers observed that, at 4 wt% polyethylene, the material would reach about 8 MPa, giving it nearly twice the strength of typical concrete. Going up to 7 wt% increased the flexural strength to around 14 MPa, comparable to any steel-reinforced concrete and at 10 wt%, it rose sharply to 23 MPa.Beyond the 10 wt% threshold, further additions of polyethylene yielded smaller gains in structural reinforcement. Though the material achieved its highest strength of 30 MPa, at 25 wt% PE. Raising the pressure from 70 MPa to 140 MPa increased strength from around 22 MPa to 27 MPa, marking an improvement of nearly 22% but when it went above 140 MPa, then it didn’t produce any additional strengthening. The study identified that the preferred range for production was a 7–10 wt% polyethylene and compaction pressure of 70–100 MPa.The final materials properties were significantly influenced by both temperature and processing duration. Before compaction, the samples were heated at 200°C and by increasing the heating duration from 10 to 30 minutes enhanced the material's strength from 14 MPa to 25 MPa, giving a 79% increase. In contrast, longer heating at 50-60 minutes would reduce the strength to around 14 MPa, as observed by researchers this decline was because of oxidation and possibly the polyethylene’s thermal decomposition, which can reduce the effective molecular weight of the polymer.The time between removing the heated mould from the oven and beginning compaction was also important. An interval of less than one minute yielded the highest strength and three to six minutes would level the strength at only 40-60% of the peak value, while an interval of ten minutes would reduce the strength by 80%. The study also found that if the materials were confined when heated, the material’s strength would reduce by 25% which meant that free expansion during heating allowed polyethylene to spread through the sand structure. This approach speaks to the issue of Portland cement production being carbon-intensive, and waste plastics are difficult to recycle. Since building materials are tolerant to minor impurities, the researchers proposed that waste plastic could potentially be used as a binder.
Article Summary: Researchers in 2020 developed a structural material through the combination of sand with only about 10 wt% polyethylene and compacting the mixture under pressure. The study published as showed by using about 10 wt polyethylene and 70–100 MPa of compaction pressure, the formulation produced flexural strength greater than typical steel-reinforced concrete.

Article Title: A Connecticut man paid $35 for a bowl at a yard sale in 2020; experts revealed it was a rare 15th-century Chinese treasure and it sold for $721,800
Article Text:
Image: AP

A $35 find at a Connecticut yard sale

Experts identify a Ming dynasty treasure

Only seven comparable bowls were known

Sotheby's estimates the bowl at up to $500,000

Fifteen bids push the price beyond expectations

A bowl made for the Yongle court

From an ordinary yard sale to a major auction

A Connecticut man paid $35 for a small blue-and-white porcelain bowl at a yard sale near New Haven in 2020, unaware that he had stumbled upon an exceptionally rare Chinese imperial-era artefact. The unnamed antiques enthusiast suspected the bowl might be special and later sent photographs to Sotheby's for an evaluation. Specialists identified it as a Ming dynasty bowl dating to the early 15th century, during the reign of the Yongle Emperor. Only seven comparable bowls were known to exist, including the Connecticut discovery. Sotheby's initially estimated that it could sell for $300,000 to $500,000. When the bowl went under the hammer in New York on March 17, 2021, it attracted 15 bids and eventually sold for $721,800, including fees.The discovery began at a yard sale in the New Haven area in 2020. The buyer, whose identity was not disclosed, was an antiques enthusiast browsing the items when he noticed the small porcelain bowl.Unlike someone who simply stumbled across an object by chance, the buyer apparently had enough knowledge to suspect that the bowl could be valuable. He paid the $35 asking price without haggling and took it home. He later contacted Sotheby's and sent photographs of the piece, asking the auction house to assess it.The decision to seek an expert opinion proved crucial. Sotheby's receives photographs and inquiries about potentially valuable objects regularly, but specialists Angela McAteer, head of the auction house's Chinese works of art department, and specialist Hang Yin recognised something unusual in the bowl. When they examined it in person, they determined that its shape, glaze, cobalt-blue decoration and other characteristics were consistent with early 15th-century Chinese porcelain.Sotheby's identified the object as an exceptional blue-and-white floral bowl from the Ming dynasty's Yongle period. The Yongle Emperor ruled from 1403 to 1424, placing the bowl's production in the early 15th century.The bowl measures approximately 6¼ inches, or 16 centimetres, in diameter. Its shape resembles a lotus bud or what is sometimes described as a chicken-heart form. The interior contains a central medallion and intricate floral and geometric decoration, while the exterior features four different flowers: lotus, peony, chrysanthemum and pomegranate.Sotheby's described the piece as a quintessential example of Yongle-period porcelain made for the imperial court. During the Yongle reign, the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced sophisticated blue-and-white porcelain, and the bowl reflects the distinctive craftsmanship and decorative style associated with that period.The bowl's age was only part of what made it remarkable. Its rarity was even more significant.Sotheby's specialists said that only six other comparable bowls were known to exist, making seven including the Connecticut example. Most were held by major museums and institutions rather than private American collections.Known examples included bowls in collections associated with the National Palace Museum in Taipei, museums in London and the National Museum of Iran in Tehran. Sotheby's said there were no other examples of the type in US museums at the time.The fact that such a scarce imperial-era object had appeared at an ordinary Connecticut yard sale made its discovery particularly striking. How the bowl reached the sale was not known. Sotheby's suggested that it may have passed through generations of a family that did not realise how unusual it was.After authentication, Sotheby's prepared the bowl for its Important Chinese Art auction in New York. The auction house placed a presale estimate of $300,000 to $500,000.That estimate represented an extraordinary jump from the $35 paid at the yard sale. At the upper estimate of $500,000, the bowl would already have been worth more than 14,000 times its purchase price.The auction listing provided extensive details about the bowl's construction and decoration. Sotheby's described its rich cobalt-blue painting, delicate floral motifs and distinctive shape, all of which helped specialists establish its relationship to Yongle-period imperial porcelain.The bowl was offered at Sotheby's New York on March 17, 2021, as part of the auction house's Important Chinese Art sale during Asia Week.Bidding quickly moved beyond the lower end of the estimate. Contemporary reports said the auction attracted 15 bids, beginning at $200,000 from an online bidder. The competition eventually pushed the hammer price to $580,000.After Sotheby's fees were added, the official price realised was $721,800. Four bidders were reported to have competed for the bowl during the auction.The final price substantially exceeded Sotheby's $500,000 upper estimate. Compared with the original $35 purchase, the $721,800 result represented more than 20,000 times what the buyer had paid.The Yongle period was an important stage in the development of Chinese blue-and-white porcelain. The imperial court encouraged new styles and high-quality production at the Jingdezhen kilns in present-day Jiangxi province.The Connecticut bowl reflects that tradition through its carefully painted floral decoration. The outside alternates lotus, peony, chrysanthemum and pomegranate blossoms with other decorative emblems, while the interior contains additional geometric and floral designs.Its small size also belies the complexity of its decoration. Despite measuring only about 16 centimetres across, the bowl contains multiple layers of painted motifs and carefully executed patterns.The buyer had paid the $35 asking price after spotting the bowl at a yard sale. Rather than leaving it as an unidentified piece of pottery, he sought professional advice and contacted Sotheby's. That decision led specialists to identify a rare Ming dynasty object that had survived for more than six centuries.The bowl's final auction price also showed the importance of rarity, craftsmanship and imperial provenance in the market for Chinese ceramics. Its appearance at a New Haven-area yard sale remains unexplained, but its subsequent examination established that the seemingly modest purchase was an exceptionally rare example of Yongle-period porcelain.On March 17, 2021, the $35 yard-sale purchase completed its extraordinary transformation when it sold at Sotheby's for $721,800 including fees.
Article Summary: A Connecticut man paid $35 for a small blue-and-white porcelain bowl at a yard sale near New Haven in 2020. He was unaware that he had stumbled upon an exceptionally rare Chinese imperial-era artefact. The unnamed antiques enthusiast suspected the bowl might be special and later sent photographs to Sotheby's for an evaluation. Specialists identified it as a Ming dynasty bowl dating to the early 15th century, during the reign of the Yongle Emperor. Only seven comparable bowls were known to exist, including the Connecticut discovery.

Article Title: In 2026, Phoenix added 19 shade roofs at busy crossings; the desert-inspired structures now give pedestrians a cooler place to wait for traffic lights
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a desert-inspired shade canopy giving pedestrians relief while they wait at a crosswalk. Credits - Gemini

Designs inspired by the desert

The importance of shade in this context

AI-generated representative image showing pedestrians waiting in the shade of a permanent canopy at an intersection during summer heat. Credits - Gemini

How much difference does it make

In July, a red pedestrian light in Phoenix is a little endurance test. The sun beats down on your neck, the pavement is hot, and many places lack trees or cover. The city's solution, completed in April 2026, consists of 19 colorful shade structures installed at major intersections and crosswalks, where pedestrians can use them while waiting for traffic signals to change. The designs take inspiration from the Sonoran Desert.The City of Phoenix states the Office of Heat Response and Mitigation partnered with the Streets Transportation Department and the Department of Arts and Culture on the project. The locations were selected for pedestrians who must wait for traffic signals to change.Three different shade designs were used, all inspired by the local desert environment. Two are variations on the saguaro blossom, one a single panel by artist Isaac Caruso, the other a multi-panel rendition by Heidi Dauphin with Studio Curiosity. The third is a butterfly design by Sara Altieri of Green Heart Creative Services. Each structure has its own look, shaped by the artists’ patterns etched in the roof panels and their choice of colour. The city's location list identifies structures with concrete bases as well as structures without them.The structures are distributed across the city, from Indian School Road and Central Avenue to Van Buren Street and 28th Street, and from Camelback Road and 23rd Avenue to Southern Avenue and 19th Avenue. The city had a public meeting in August 2024 to share plans and hear feedback.The project was not without its detractors. The project was funded with federal American Rescue Plan Act money, and Heat Response and Mitigation Director David Hondula said the funding requirements helped determine where structures could be installed. Councilwoman Betty Guardado expressed disappointment that District 5 would receive only one structure.It’s not easy to dismiss the health argument. In 2025, the yearly report of the Maricopa County public health department found 430 deaths attributable to heat. It’s down from 608 in 2024 and a record 645 in 2023, but it’s still a terrible toll. That won’t be prevented by a shade canopy at a crossing by itself, but it’s aimed at a place where people can’t just walk away from the sun.Shade science tells us the roofs are worth the effort. Air temperature doesn’t vary much between sun and shade, but what a body feels does. Air temperature may vary by only a couple of degrees between sun and shade, but physiological equivalent temperature, a measure of how hot conditions feel to the body, can vary by about 20 degrees in summer, said ASU urban climatologist Ariane Middel. She said constructed shade structures work in ASU studies for regions where trees have a particularly difficult time growing and don’t need water.But shade is not a complete solution to extreme heat. An ASU field study led by Middel found that shade from photovoltaic canopies and trees improved outdoor thermal comfort in Tempe, showing why reducing direct solar exposure matters even when the surrounding air remains hot.The project covers only a small part of Phoenix's pedestrian network, while trees remain important to the city's longer-term shade strategy. The crossings provide relief at that one place where pedestrians have to pause in the sun, subject to the signal. That is a modest change that can help pedestrians crossing Phoenix in the summer.
Article Summary: 19 shade structures will be installed at major intersections and crosswalks in Phoenix, Arizona. The designs take inspiration from the Sonoran Desert. Each structure has its own look, shaped by the artists’ patterns etched in the roof panels and their choice of colour.

Article Title: St. Anthony Village buried a 500,000-gallon tank beside a Minnesota road; it now catches runoff and reuses the water to irrigate City Park and City Hall
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing stormwater runoff being captured and diverted into a water-reuse system. Credits - Gemini

Why runoff is a problem

What the tank does

AI-generated representative image showing reclaimed stormwater being reused to irrigate a municipal park. Credits - Gemini

Maintenance and Lessons

Rain washes pollutants from roads into the stormwater system. Along the way, runoff can pick up debris, oil, litter and leaves before entering the stormwater system. It was intercepted by St. Anthony Village, a small town in the Twin Cities region of Minnesota. St. Anthony Village installed a 500,000-gallon underground storage tank that collects runoff from nearby streets, buildings and parking lots. It collects runoff from nearby streets and parking lots and stores it for later reuse.According to the City of St. Anthony Village , the facility was the first of its kind when installed. The city reports a 91% reduction in runoff volume during the growing season, a 77.5% reduction in phosphorus load from the site and savings of about 4.6 million gallons of potable water or groundwater for irrigation each year.The city says stormwater runoff is a major source of pollution to surface waters, while runoff from rooftops, pavement and lawns can carry garbage, oil and debris into storm drains and nearby water bodies. Silver Lake is on Minnesota’s Impaired Waters List, and stormwater systems in St. Anthony and surrounding communities can carry runoff directly into local lakes, rivers and streams. Phosphorus is of particular concern since it feeds the algae in lakes, and the city is responsible for two watersheds that expect to see continuous improvement.The system, which catches, cleans and reuses runoff from a 15-acre area around City Hall, was funded by the Mississippi Watershed Management Organisation . Water is stored in a 500,000-gallon underground reservoir before being reused on about 20 acres of municipal land. The city calls that park Central Park, but some state documents call it City Park.The tank has another function: it also receives backwash from the adjacent water treatment plant and filters that water for reuse. Solid pollutants settle to the bottom of the tank, while the stored water is filtered and then pumped to the adjacent ball fields and City Hall campus for irrigation. A Metropolitan Council handbook gives the city's water tower a capacity of 250,000 gallons, half the capacity of the underground reservoir.If pollution settles out, that means the tank collects it. When the city drained the tank for maintenance in November 2015, it took days to pump the water down and left thigh-thick sludge on the floor, the mayor subsequently wrote. It also shows that the system requires regular cleaning.Minnesota's Stormwater Manual uses St. Anthony Village as a large-scale example of stormwater reuse and notes that stored water from cisterns can be used for non-potable purposes such as irrigation. The same guidance cites Tucson, Arizona, as a separate example, where commercial developments are required to meet at least half of their irrigation needs with harvested rainwater. The project shows how captured stormwater can be reused for municipal irrigation while reducing demand for other water supplies. It does need frequent cleaning and room to grow, but the city’s own results suggest it has been worth the investment.
Article Summary: St. Anthony Village, Minnesota, installed a 500,000-gallon underground storage tank that collects runoff from nearby streets, buildings and parking lots. Water is stored in the tank before being reused on about 20 acres of municipal land. The city reports a 91% reduction in runoff volume during the growing season, a 77.5% Reduction in phosphorus load from the site and savings of about 4.6 million gallons of potable water or groundwater.

Article Title: In 1964, a Virginia widow fought to save her Frank Lloyd Wright home from Interstate 66; it was dismantled piece by piece, moved 13 miles and rebuilt at Woodlawn, where it still stands
Article Text:
A dream house

It was in 1939 that Loren Pope wrote to the architect Frank Lloyd Wright, begging him for a home for himself and his wife Charlotte

Saving a home

A lasting legacy

The home was dismantled, moved, and reconstructed 13 miles away from Falls Church to Alexandria.

Sixty years ago, a house was reconstructed at Woodlawn, a National Trust-owned property outside of Washington, DC, after a historic and hard-fought battle to save it from destruction. Originally built in Falls Church, Virginia for Loren and Charlotte Pope, the 1,200-square-foot Frank Lloyd Wright home was under threat due to the construction of the new Interstate 66, but was saved by a historic hard-fought battle led by Marjorie Leighey, a 57-year-old widow, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Today, thousands of guests visit the unique house, the only property designed by America's greatest architect that is open to the public in the National Capital region.It was in 1939 that Loren Pope wrote to the architect Frank Lloyd Wright, begging him for a home for himself and his wife Charlotte. In response, Wright designed a house in his Usonian style- relatively small, built from everyday materials like wood and concrete and designed in harmony with natural surroundings.At the end of 1946, after living in the house for five years, the Popes put a for-sale ad in the papers and two weeks later, the house came to be owned by Robert and Marjorie Leighey.While Robert was the one who first fell in love with the house, his wife, Marjorie, remained sceptical.She was eventually won over by the way the home married the interior and exterior and as an avid gardener, she loved the way the house allowed her to see the surrounding landscape through a new lens. “From the time I was five, I can remember wanting a house that was right with the earth,” she later said. They built a shed outside for items that could not fit in the houseIn 1961, the couple learnt that the new Interstate Highway 66 would pass directly through the property they had lived in for the past 15 years. This meant the government planned to seize their land and demolish their house. But all the concerns were put on the back burner as Robert battled an illness that eventually led to his death on July 29, 1963.Two months after Robert died, Marjorie was officially notified by Virginia's Department of Highways that the interstate was slated to be paved through her living room. Springing into action, she hired a lawyer to delay the government and recognising the abode's cultural importance, asked help from Terry and Hamilton Morton, preservationists who worked for the National Trust for Historic Preservation. At the time, the preservation community tended to focus on saving much older properties, but Marjorie insisted that the 22-year-old house deserved the same protections as properties built 150 years earlier.“It does seem like at least part of her thought in wanting to save the house was also saving memories she has of her husband,” observed Elizabeth Reese, senior manager of public programs at Woodlawn and the Pope-Leighey House. “That demonstrates that for a lot of people, doing larger acts of public service comes from a very personal place.”Along with Marjorie, preservationists, National Park Service employees, politicians and neighbours all came together to find a way to ensure that the Pope-Leighey House lived on. Recognising the value in gathering public support, Marjorie encouraged the press coverage, giving interviews that pressed for others to join her cause. “I’m not doing this for myself, but for architects, students, and people building their own homes,” she told the Virginia Sun in 1964. Loren Pope now begged the community to stop the destruction of an architectural treasure. In a letter to the editor of the Washington Post, he wrote that only a society with a “barbarian set of values…could even entertain a proposal to let a road threaten [a Wright house].”One of the people inspired by Marjorie’s determination was Secretary of the Interior Stewart Udall. It was he and Marjorie, along with preservationists from the National Park Service and the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who finally devised a plan for saving the Pope-Leighy House.The group quickly realised that while the I-66 plans could not change, the house itself could be moved. After being offered various options, Marjorie chose Woodlawn as its new location, in part because the landscape reminded her of Falls Church. Brick by brick, the house was carefully demolished, transported, and rebuilt on the National Trust property, where Marjorie lived in it until her death. The near-loss of the Pope-Leighey House was one of many efforts that inspired Udall and preservationists across the country to pursue a national law to preserve historic buildings. Thanks in part to his and Marjorie’s efforts, President Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act in 1966.After fighting for so long to ensure the survival of her home, Marjorie moved to Kyoto, Japan, to become an Episcopal missionary in September 1964, and did not witness the dismantling, move, and reconstruction of her house 13 miles away from Falls Church to Alexandria.Just seven years later, the house was listed on the National Register. Marjorie moved back to the country and to her home in 1969. She continued to live in it until her death, and welcomed the many visitors who came to see not only the house, but the woman who saved it.Thanks to Marjorie Leighey's efforts and the tools instituted by the National Historic Preservation Act, dozens of sites of cultural and historical significance have been saved, both by individuals and government entities. “She was an accidental preservationist,” Reese said. “Hopefully, when people visit this exhibit, [they ask themselves], ‘what kinds of personal things can I do that might make a larger impact?’ “
Article Summary: The 1,200-square-foot Frank Lloyd Wright home was under threat due to the construction of the new Interstate 66. It was saved by a historic hard-fought battle led by Marjorie Leighey, a 57-year-old widow. The Pope-Leighey House was dismantled, moved, and reconstructed 13 miles away from Falls Church to Alexandria.

Article Title: Ball State buried about 3,600 geothermal wells beneath its Indiana campus; the system now heats and cools 47 buildings and saves roughly $2 million a year
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image. Credits - Gemini

Why did the university dig

How the ground does the work

AI-generated representative image showing geothermal heat-pump equipment transferring thermal energy through Ball State University’s campus-wide heating and cooling network. Credits - Gemini

How the system works

For nearly 70 years, Ball State University in Muncie, Indiana, relied on coal to heat its campus during winter. The campus heating plant had four coal-fired boilers that burned, according to later estimates, about 36,000 tons of coal a year to keep classrooms and residence halls warm. But as the equipment aged and the cost of installing a new fossil fuel boiler increased, university leaders began to look at renewable options instead. The university has installed a campus-wide geothermal network that now supplies heating and cooling across much of the campus.According to the US Department of Energy, it is one of the country’s largest ground-source geothermal heating and cooling systems. Construction began in 2009 to replace four coal-fired boilers and eventually provide heating and cooling to 47 buildings across the campus. Geothermal heat pumps had long been used to heat and cool individual buildings, but applying the technology at this campus scale was unprecedented at the time.Coal was turning into a bad investment. The boilers were getting older and less dependable, and the cost of a new fossil fuel unit would have increased with each passing year. The university decided to transform the entire campus after a proof of concept trial persuaded the team that a ground source heat pump system could supply both hot and chilled water.Not everyone saw that as wise. Two reputable geothermal system designers informed project manager Jim Lowe they weren't sure a system this big would be practical and effective, according to Ball State's own magazine. Drilling started in July 2009 after Lowe refused to accept that. The remaining coal-fired boilers were shut down in March 2014. The bill arrived at $83 million, covered by state appropriations and federal grants, including Recovery Act money.A few feet below the surface, the ground remains close to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, providing a relatively stable temperature that engineers can use as a source of heat in winter and a place to reject heat in summer. About 3,600 boreholes, each roughly 400 feet deep, were drilled across campus, and every one holds a loop of pipe sealed in grout. Because this is a closed-loop system, fresh water circulates through the pipes without ever touching natural groundwater.In winter, heat pumps extract heat from that fluid and transfer it into the buildings. In summer, the process reverses: heat is extracted from the buildings and released back into the ground. There are two district energy stations, one north and one south, with four heat pump chillers, each of 2,500 tonnes. About 10 miles of distribution piping connect the energy stations to campus buildings, while the borehole fields contain roughly 1,000 miles of smaller geothermal piping.The system has also substantially reduced the university's carbon footprint by replacing coal-fired heating. The campus is avoiding the burning of coal, thus saving roughly 85,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, along with reductions in sulphur dioxide, particulate matter and coal ash, the engineers’ design summary said.It's not all one-sided. Ball State's project analysis found that the geothermal system could reduce overall energy use and carbon dioxide emissions compared with continuing to rely on the coal-fired boilers. The project also required a substantial upfront investment, making state and federal support important to its development.But the initiative has attracted interest far beyond Indiana. Ball State said tour groups from Germany, Iceland, Japan and South Korea had visited the two energy stations. One of the project engineers later worked on a geothermal system at Ford Motor Co.'s world headquarters.The lesson is practical for colleges and towns facing the same issue. A complete loop of wells can replace coal for heating and cooling at the district level and can pay off in lower running costs and healthier air, if there is money to cover the drilling. Ball State was among the first universities to use a geothermal system at this scale, and the boreholes beneath the campus now perform much of the heating and cooling work once supplied by coal.
Article Summary: Ball State University in Muncie, Indiana, relied on coal to heat its campus during winter. The campus heating plant had four coal-fired boilers that burned, according to later estimates, about 36,000 tons of coal a year to keep classrooms and residence halls warm. As the equipment aged and the cost of installing a new fossil fuel boiler increased, university leaders began to look at renewable options. The university has installed a campus-wide geothermal network that now supplies heating and cooling across much of the campus.

Article Title: Kentucky woman started a $300 eBay side hustle in 2011, left her $35,000 insurance job in 2014; 10 years later, Pink Lily reached $141 million
Article Text:
PC: CNBC

How a $300 eBay clothing side hustle became Pink Lily

How Tori Gerbig took Pink Lily from eBay to its own website

Tori and Chris Gerbig take Pink Lily full-time as sales surge

PC: CNBC

From an eBay shop to a larger retail operation

Social media became part of the retail model

Customers were also used as brand ambassadors

Pink Lily bought entire inventories to offer exclusive clothing

What started in a living room had become a $141 million business

In 2011, Tori and Chris Gerbig were not setting out to build a large fashion retailer. They were a young Kentucky couple with an interest in affordable women’s clothing and about $300 to put into a small online venture. Writing for CNBC in 2022, Tori revealed that she was still working in insurance, at that time while the clothing business ran alongside their jobs and family life. What began with listings on eBay gradually developed into Pink Lily, an online fashion company based in Bowling Green, Kentucky. Ten years after that first investment, the business reported $141 million in gross sales for the year, illustrating how a modest online shop had grown into a sizeable retail operation.The Gerbigs launched their eBay shop in 2011 after noticing that finding fashionable women's clothes at relatively low prices was not always straightforward. They put roughly $300 into their first batch of clothing and accessories, buying stock through a wholesale website.At that stage, the operation was deliberately small. Tori continued working her insurance job while she and Chris handled orders from their living room.There was little in the way of fixed business overhead, although shipping costs had to be covered.Their approach to pricing was fairly simple at first. Tori had no previous experience in retail pricing, so she based prices on what she would have been willing to pay as a customer. The business was not producing anything close to the figures it would later report, but it was generating enough to keep the experiment going.During the first few years, monthly profits generally ranged between $300 and $1,000. Rather than treating that money as household income, the couple used it to pay down student loans and buy more stock.The business began to take on a different shape as Tori spent more time building relationships with suppliers. She travelled to Los Angeles to meet vendors and began attending trade shows, giving the couple access to a wider selection of products.In 2013, Tori also created a Facebook group to promote the clothing to potential customers. The group helped create a direct line between the business and shoppers, particularly around Bowling Green, Kentucky.That year proved important for the company. The Gerbigs had accumulated about $20,000 from the business, which they used to build an official website for Pink Lily. The move took the operation beyond its original eBay model and gave the couple a dedicated place to sell their growing range. The change was followed by a sharp increase in revenue.By May 2014, Pink Lily was generating more than $100,000 in monthly revenue. After three years of running the business alongside her employment, Tori left her insurance sales job of earning $35,000 per year and began working on Pink Lily full-time.Chris followed several months later. His role centred on the company's finances and operations, while the business continued expanding its product range and customer base. Pink Lily finished 2014 with more than $4 million in revenue. The figures were a long way from the $300 monthly investment that had started the venture just a few years earlier.The company continued to grow over the following years. By 2019, Pink Lily had recorded $70 million in total sales and brought in a minority investment to help support its expansion.By the time Gerbig described the company's progress in 2022, Pink Lily was selling more than 11,000 products on its website and had also opened a physical shop. The business employed about 250 full-time workers in Bowling Green, where it had become one of the larger employers in the area.The Gerbigs still attended trade shows, but Pink Lily had developed a core group of vendor relationships and was working with partners on custom designs. That represented a considerable shift from the couple's original model of buying clothing wholesale and listing individual items on eBay. The company had developed its own retail identity and a much larger supply operation.Then came the sales figure that put the scale of that expansion into perspective. In 2021, Pink Lily generated $141 million in gross sales, according to Gerbig's account published by CNBC in February 2022.Pink Lily's growth was also tied to how the company used social media. Rather than treating platforms such as Instagram simply as advertising channels, the business used its audience to gather feedback about products and potential brands. Customers were asked what they wanted to see on the website and in the shop. The company could then use those responses when deciding which products to stock.The strategy extended to customers sharing photographs of their purchases. Pink Lily sent orders in branded bags and encouraged shoppers to post their outfits using the company's hashtag. Some of that customer content was then featured on the Pink Lily website.Tori Gerbig said, “At first, it was just a fun hobby. Little did I know, 10 years later, my husband Chris and I would be running Pink Lily full-time. Last year, our online clothing business generated $141 million in gross sales. And today, our social media audience has grown to 3.6 million followers.”Pink Lily developed a paid ambassador programme around some of its longstanding customers. Participants received a 10% commission on sales generated through their promotion of the brand. It was not a small part of the company's marketing activity. Gerbig said the ambassador programme generated about $7.5 million in sales in 2021.The model gave Pink Lily another way of reaching shoppers through people who already bought its products. Instead of relying entirely on conventional advertising, the company incorporated existing customers into its sales and promotional system.As Pink Lily became larger, the Gerbigs also looked for ways to make some of its merchandise less interchangeable with products available from other retailers. In certain cases, the company would purchase a vendor's entire inventory of a particular item. That meant the same product could not simply appear elsewhere through another retailer using the same supplier. This approach helped Pink Lily assemble collections that were specific to its own store rather than relying exclusively on products that shoppers could find across multiple online retailers.The distance between Pink Lily's first year and its reported 2021 sales is substantial. The company began with about $300 worth of inventory, a living-room workspace and two people managing the operation around existing commitments. Three years later, Tori had left her insurance career after the side business began generating six-figure monthly revenue. Chris then joined her full-time, and the company moved from a small eBay seller into its own online retail operation.By 2021, Pink Lily had reached $141 million in gross sales, employed around 250 people and sold thousands of products through its website and physical shop. The business had also taken outside minority investment and developed a network of suppliers and customer ambassadors.
Article Summary: Tori and Chris Gerbig started Pink Lily as a small eBay side hustle in 2011. After three years of running the business, Tori left her insurance job to work full-time. Pink Lily now has 11,000 products on its website and has opened a physical shop.

Article Title: In 1899, nine-year-old Thomas Gilcrease received 160 acres; 18 years later, it had 32 producing oil wells, and his wealth later helped build Tulsa's Gilcrease Museum
Article Text:
​Financial troubles forced Gilcrease to give up control of his collection and museum to the City of Tulsa in 1955.

Gilcrease becomes art collector

Some of the collection at Gilcrease museum

Building the dream museum

Tulsa secures ollection

Thomas Gilcrease was just nine-year-old when he became eligible for a 160-acre land allotment in Oklahoma through his Creek tribal membership in 1899. The land, near present-day Glenpool, later became part of the Glenn Pool oilfield, where oil was discovered in 1905. By 1917, 32 producing wells were operating on his property, giving Gilcrease the income to continue his education and eventually build a career in the oil industry. That wealth later supported his growing interest in American Indian history, art and culture.Gilcrease was born in 1890, in Robeline, Louisiana, the eldest child of his parents, according to Oklahoma Historical Society. His family moved to the Creek Nation in Oklahoma Territory soon after his birth and eventually settled at Wealaka. His Creek ancestry came through his mother, while his father was non-Indian.His name was entered on the Creek tribal rolls when he was nine which made him eligible for the 160-acre allotment under the Dawes Commission process. At the time, the value of the land was not yet tied to the oil wealth that would later come from it. Six years after Gilcrease received the allotment, the Glenn Pool oilfield was discovered in 1905 and by 1917, the property had 32 producing oil wells.The income from the land helped Gilcrease continue his education. He had attended rural one-room schools before studying at Bacone College and the Kansas State Teacher's College in Emporia.At Bacone, one of his teachers was Alexander Posey, who taught Gilcrease about the Trail of Tears and American Indian leaders such as Sequoyah and Sitting Bull. He learnt about making bows and arrows, hunting and the operations of the Creek National Council at Okmulgee. These lessons became part of a wider interest in American Indian history that remained important to Gilcrease throughout his life.Oil became an important part of Gilcrease's working life. He eventually worked in several fields, including ranching, farming, banking and the oil industry. In 1922, he founded the Gilcrease Oil Company. His company later brought in numerous wells in Oklahoma, Texas and Kansas.Gilcrease also discovered a new oil-producing strata near Wetumka. It became known as the Gilcrease sand. His business interests expanded further, and he obtained controlling interests in several banks, including the Fourth National Bank of Tulsa, the Bank of Bixby and state banks in Coweta and Wagoner.While his oil business was growing, so was his interest in art. Gilcrease bought his first painting, Rural Courtship by Daniel Ridgway Knight, in 1912. He later travelled to Europe to study fine art and petroleum. According to the Gilcrease museum. During these trips, he became interested in building a collection connected to American Indian history and the American West.Gilcrease gathered American Indian art and artefacts, books, manuscripts, maps and other historical material. He also became involved in archaeological work and personally excavated Indian archaeological sites in the United States and Mesoamerica.Gilcrease's collecting became more active during the 1930s and 1940s. In 1942, he established the Thomas Gilcrease Foundation to gather, maintain and preserve material related to American Indians. A year later, he opened his first museum in San Antonio, Texas.Gilcrease had moved his company headquarters to San Antonio in 1937 to be closer to his major field operations. However, the museum did not attract enough public interest there. He closed the display in 1947 and moved his collection back to Tulsa.In May 1949, Gilcrease opened a new museum in Tulsa. The building stood beside his home west of downtown. The collection continued to grow as he acquired paintings, books, photographs, manuscripts and other historical material.One of the major additions came in 1944, when Gilcrease purchased Dr Philip G Cole's Western art collection. The purchase included 636 works of art, along with books, photographs and archival material. It also brought paintings by Frederic Remington and works by Charles M Russell into his collection.Another major acquisition came in 1948, when Gilcrease acquired the estate of landscape painter Thomas Moran. It contained about 2,000 works of art, including watercolours of the Yellowstone region of Montana and Wyoming. He also acquired an important collection of art and correspondence connected to George Catlin, as well as works by Alfred Jacob Miller.Gilcrease's collection also included works by artists such as Winslow Homer, John Singer Sargent and James McNeill Whistler. During visits to the artists' colony at Taos, New Mexico, he bought paintings directly from artists including Ernest Blumenschein and Bert Phillips. He also collected the work of Native American artists including Acee Blue Eagle, Woody Crumbo and Willard Stone.The scale of Gilcrease's collecting eventually created financial difficulties. By 1953, he was financially strained and owed about $2.5 million to business associates, galleries and art brokers for various acquisitions.The City of Tulsa then organised a bond issue in 1954 to pay Gilcrease's debts and secure his collection for the community. In 1955, Gilcrease transferred the title to his collection to the city. The museum was renamed the Thomas Gilcrease Institute of American History and Art.In 1958, Gilcrease also deeded the museum buildings and more than 13 acres of land to the community. Revenue from some of his oil properties was committed towards repaying the original bond amount. That repayment was completed in 1985.Gilcrease, however, continued collecting after the transfer of his collection to Tulsa. His interest in archaeology and ethnology also led him to support field excavations of Indian mounds in the Mississippi Valley. Material from those excavations and his later collecting eventually reached the museum through a bequest after his death in 1962.The collection continued to expand after Gilcrease's death. The museum now houses more than 12,000 works of fine art, while its Helmerich Center for American Research holds about 100,000 rare books, manuscripts and other archival materials.The museum's collections also include more than a quarter of a million artefacts related to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas. The collection had grown to include 10,000 works of American Indian and related art, 250,000 artefacts and 100,000 rare books when the collection was presented to the people of Tulsa in 1955.
Article Summary: Thomas Gilcrease was born in 1890 in Robeline, Louisiana. His family moved to the Creek Nation in Oklahoma Territory soon after his birth. He became eligible for a 160-acre land allotment in 1899. The land later became part of the Glenn Pool oilfield, where oil was discovered in 1905. By 1917, 32 producing wells were operating on his property. That income helped him continue his education and build a career in the oil industry. He also became interested in American Indian history and art.

Article Title: In 2005, as Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans, an Audubon Zoo curator and 11 staff members stayed with the animals; careful planning meant the zoo’s animals survived the storm
Article Text:
View of the eyewall of Hurricane Katrina taken on Aug. 28, 2005. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Curator

Dan Maloney

and a staff of 11 stayed at Audubon Zoo through Katrina

Katrina made landfall near Buras, Louisiana, on August 29, 2005

Tropical Cyclone Report: Hurricane Katrina, 23-30 August 2005

Most of New Orleans saw Category 1 or 2 winds

Out of nearly 1,500 animals, a raccoon, two young otters and a Bali monitor were lost

The zoo's plan called for stockpiled fuel and food

The Aquarium of the Americas lost about 10,000 of its 15,000 animals when life support failed

Audubon Zoo, New Orleans USA. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Did Harvey Learn from Katrina? Initial Observations of the Response to Companion Animals during Hurricane Harvey

Accounts of the staff count and the losses differ slightly

When a hurricane approaches a city, residents are usually advised to evacuate. For a zoo manager, however, evacuation is rarely an option, because animals cannot simply be loaded into a car. This is what happened during Hurricane Katrina when a small group of Audubon Zoo employees chose to stay rather than evacuate. The current paper will focus on who chose to stay, what happened to the city because of the hurricane, how the zoo residents survived, and how Katrina shaped later planning for animals in disasters, particularly for household pets.According to PBS Nature's Katrina's Animal Rescue, curator Dan Maloney and a staff of 11 stayed with the animals right through the hurricane. It credits the zoo's high elevation and the staff's careful emergency planning for the animals' survival. An NPR report from that November calls Maloney the zoo's general curator and says the zookeepers rode out the storm in the reptile house. The PBS feature adds that Maloney later asked soldiers stationed at the zoo to walk the grounds when off duty, and that the elephants and primates in particular began to respond., by Richard Knabb, Jamie Rhome and Daniel Brown, gives the storm's track. Katrina peaked as a Category 5 hurricane with 150-knot winds on August 28. Afterward, it weakened and made landfall near Buras at 1110 UTC on August 29 with maximum winds of 110 knots and minimum pressure of 920 millibars. Later on August 29, the National Hurricane Center's report says, Katrina made a second landfall near the Louisiana/Mississippi border, still as a Category 3 hurricane.The same report also indicates that much of New Orleans probably saw sustained winds at the level of a Category 1 or Category 2 hurricane, despite being a Category 3 at landfall. The larger issue was the water; the storm surge was 15-19 feet in eastern New Orleans, the flood walls were overtopped/breached, and 80% of the city flooded to a depth of up to 20 feet. According to Britannica, the Army Corps of Engineers pumped the last of the floodwaters out of New Orleans on October 11, 2005, about 43 days after Katrina made landfall. The zoo sits on elevated ground. Twenty years later, in a 2025 interview with WHAS, Maloney, now director of the Louisville Zoo, recalled that the zoo did not flood and that broken tree branches were the most visible damage. He also said his team lived at the zoo for two months, a difficult time.According to NPR, quoting Maloney, the total number of animals at the zoo is almost 1,500, and the list of the losses goes like this: there was one raccoon who drowned, two young otters that passed away several days after the storm and one Bali monitor that disappeared. According to NBC News, Audubon Zoo reopened on the Friday after Thanksgiving in 2005, the first day it had been open since Hurricane Katrina. According to NPR, without revenue the zoo furloughed three-quarters of its overall staff, and the animal care staff went from nearly 65 to 35 people.According to a report on Mongabay from the week of the hurricane, a quote by zoo spokeswoman Sarah Burnette says that "the zoo has been in close coordination with Miami MetroZoo following Hurricane Andrew and has since revised its hurricane response plan". Prior to Katrina, the zoo had prepared a supply of fuel and other food supplies. This was important because according to the National Hurricane Center report, Katrina resulted in about three million people being without electricity, for a period of about several weeks.As for the aquarium located next to the aquarium in this case, it is clear how the storm could impact the building relying on its mechanisms. According to NBC News, about 10,000 aquatic animals at the Audubon Aquarium of the Americas died because of the hurricane. Among the survivors were a green sea turtle, 19 penguins, two sea otters and an anaconda.Katrina also changed policy., by Steve Glassey in Animals, interviewed six key officials involved in the response to Hurricane Harvey in 2017. They were queried regarding the effectiveness of the federal PETS Act, which followed the hurricane. The act helped encourage evacuation planning that includes pets alongside their owners. Another observation made by the author was the poor development of the plans as per the requirements of that act and also the unresolved lessons of previous emergencies. The study looks at household pets rather than zoos and relies on a small sample of six officials, so it cannot show how the Audubon Zoo experience shaped zoo planning. It does show that planning for animals in disasters moved into government policy after Katrina, and that gaps in that planning were still being worked out in 2017.Information about Audubon Zoo is mostly first-hand. Accounts of how many people stayed differ. PBS Nature reported that Maloney and a staff of 11 stayed with the animals, while WHAS reported in 2025 that Maloney and 14 others stayed. The sources do not explain the difference. Information about animal loss is taken directly from Maloney.
Article Summary: Katrina made landfall near Buras, Louisiana, on August 29, 2005. Out of nearly 1,500 animals, a raccoon, two young otters and a Bali monitor were lost. The Aquarium of the Americas lost about 10,000 of its 15,000 animals.

Article Title: A New Jersey woman paid $25 for a mouldy table at a garage sale; 30 years later, it was identified as a rare 18th-century card table made by John Seymour & Son and sold for $541,500
Article Text:
From a $25 garage-sale table to a rare 18th-century discovery

Experts identify a rare Federal-period table

The $25 table was appraised at up to $300,000

The table heads to Sotheby's

From a garage sale to a $541,500 auction

Why the original condition mattered

A $25 purchase becomes an American furniture landmark

A New Jersey schoolteacher who bought a mouldy, pitch-black table at a garage sale for just $25 ended up owning a rare piece of American furniture worth more than half a million dollars. Claire Wiegand-Beckmann purchased the table roughly three decades before it appeared on Antiques Roadshow, when she was moving into a new home and wanted a small table. She initially saw little reason to believe it was valuable. But when furniture expert Leigh Keno examined it in Secaucus, New Jersey, in 1997, he discovered an original maker's label identifying it as the work of Boston cabinetmakers John and Thomas Seymour. The table was later sold at Sotheby's for $490,000, with the buyer's premium bringing the total to $541,500.Wiegand-Beckmann came across the table at a garage sale in New Jersey while she was moving into a new house. She told Antiques Roadshow that she needed a small table and thought the piece might work for the space.It was hardly an obvious treasure. She recalled that it was “pitch black” and “a moldy mess” when she saw it outside at the sale.The seller had priced it at $30, but Wiegand-Beckmann said she had only $25 with her. The seller agreed to accept the lower amount, allowing her to take the table home.The purchase was made roughly 30 years before her appearance on Antiques Roadshow. For years, the table was simply a piece of furniture in her Bergen County home. At the time she bought it, there was no indication that the seemingly battered table was a significant example of early American furniture.The turning point came in 1997, when Antiques Roadshow held an event in Secaucus, New Jersey. Wiegand-Beckmann decided to bring the table along to see whether experts could tell her more about it.The table reportedly arrived in an unusual fashion. Because it was awkward and wobbly, Wiegand-Beckmann brought it into the event upside down on a cart. That made the object look even less like an important piece of antique furniture.It was examined by furniture specialist Leigh Keno, who immediately began looking at its construction, decorative inlay and other characteristics. But one detail proved especially important: the table still had its original maker's label.The label read John Seymour and Son, Creek Square, Boston. Keno explained that surviving furniture with an original label from the makers was exceptionally rare.Keno identified the piece as a Federal inlaid mahogany demi-lune card table made by John and Thomas Seymour, Boston cabinetmakers working in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.The table is dated to about 1794. PBS classifies it as an 18th-century piece and identifies its material as mahogany. Keno highlighted its figured mahogany, satinwood inlay and distinctive decorative details as evidence of its quality.The Seymour name was particularly significant. John and Thomas Seymour were prominent Boston furniture makers whose work was produced for wealthy families of the period. The surviving label gave specialists an unusually direct connection between the table and its makers.Keno told Wiegand-Beckmann that the table was an exceptional example of Federal furniture. Its craftsmanship, original features and maker's label all contributed to its importance.The discovery transformed Wiegand-Beckmann's expectations. When Keno examined the table in 1997, the initial auction estimate was $200,000 to $300,000. The appraiser suggested that on a particularly good day it could potentially bring $300,000.That was already an extraordinary increase from the $25 garage-sale price.PBS later updated the auction valuation for the piece to 400,000-600,000 in its records. The broadcaster also notes that valuations can change over time depending on market conditions and the circumstances of a sale.The original $25 purchase price therefore represented only a tiny fraction of what specialists believed the table could command at auction.After the Antiques Roadshow appraisal, Wiegand-Beckmann contacted Keno about selling the table. The process eventually took it to Sotheby's in New York, where it was offered as part of the auction house's Important Americana furniture and folk art sale in January 1998.The auction attracted collectors interested in American furniture. Bidding quickly moved far beyond the original estimate.According to PBS's later account of the auction, bidding reached $490,000, at which point the table was sold. The $490,000 figure was the hammer price. Once Sotheby's buyer's premium was added, the total selling price reached $541,500.The auction result was described by PBS as a world record for Federal furniture at the time.The transformation was extraordinary. Wiegand-Beckmann had paid $25 for a table that looked dirty, damaged and unremarkable. Around three decades later, that same piece became a highly sought-after example of Federal-period American furniture.The difference between the purchase price and auction result was enormous. The $541,500 final price, including the buyer's premium, was 21,660 times the $25 that Wiegand-Beckmann had originally paid.The table's value was not simply a consequence of its age. Its rarity, original label, original finish, craftsmanship and association with John and Thomas Seymour all played important roles. Keno specifically noted that the label was unusually valuable evidence because labelled examples of the makers' work were rare.One of the unusual aspects of the story is that the table's battered appearance could easily have encouraged its owner to clean or refinish it extensively.Wiegand-Beckmann told the Antiques Roadshow team that she had used linseed oil and turpentine on the table but did not refinish it. That proved significant because retaining its original finish helped preserve the characteristics that specialists valued.Keno later explained that the table's rarity, original label and original finish were among the factors that made it such an important piece.The story has remained one of Antiques Roadshow's most memorable discoveries because the table looked so ordinary when Wiegand-Beckmann bought it. She had gone to a garage sale looking for a small piece of furniture, negotiated the price down to what she could afford and took home what appeared to be a battered old table.Instead, she had acquired a rare example of Federal-period craftsmanship by two important Boston cabinetmakers.
Article Summary: Claire Wiegand-Beckmann came across the table at a garage sale in New Jersey while she was moving into a new house. She initially saw little reason to believe it was valuable. But when furniture expert Leigh Keno examined it in Secaucus, New Jersey, in 1997, he discovered an original maker's label identifying it as the work of Boston cabinetmakers John and Thomas Seymour. The table was later sold at Sotheby's for $490,000.

Article Title: Jail, isolation, crackdown: Why Pakistan’s establishment has failed to break Imran Khan
Article Text:
Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023 (File photo)

How Imran Khan got here

Why Imran Khan matters

Imran Khan: From cricket captain to PM to inmate

How state failed to marginalise Imran Khan politically

Imran Khan: PTI's 'red line'

The 'persecution' of Imran Khan

Main legal cases against Imran Khan

Imran Khan: A case that resonates beyond politics

The state’s struggle to marginalise Imran Khan

Islamabad had prepared for another confrontation. Roads were blocked, security forces deployed and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters were expected to march towards the capital demanding the release of their jailed leader, Imran Khan Then, days before the September 27 protest, PTI postponed the march until October 4, temporarily easing the pressure on the government.But the roads can be reopened and the barricades removed. The political problem surrounding Imran Khan is proving harder to clear.The former prime minister has now spent more than three years behind bars. The establishment has used imprisonment, restrictions on his contact with the outside world, scores of legal cases and a crackdown on his supporters. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics. PTI-backed independents won the largest number of directly elected national assembly seats in the 2024 general election, and his supporters continue to mobilise around demands for his release.The postponed Islamabad march is therefore less an end to the latest confrontation than another pause in a political standoff that has survived elections, convictions and imprisonment.Imran Khan retired from international cricket in 1992, shortly after leading Pakistan to its first and, so far, only 50-over Cricket World Cup title. Four years later, in 1996, he formally entered politics by founding the PTI.His political breakthrough finally came after the 2018 general election, when the PTI emerged as the single-largest party and he became prime minister. His rise to power was widely seen by rivals and analysts as having benefited from the backing of Pakistan’s military, the country’s most powerful institution, although both Khan and the military denied that the army had helped bring him to power.That relationship subsequently deteriorated. In April 2022, the opposition brought a parliamentary no-confidence vote against Imran Khan, which he lost and was thus removed from office.He has since faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged, while he has consistently denied wrongdoing.Imran Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has remained behind bars since then. Yet his incarceration has done little to diminish his presence in Pakistan’s public life or erase him from the public consciousness.Thanks to his cricket career, Imran Khan was already a well-known public figure before entering politics. Following his retirement, he gained further goodwill by giving Pakistan its first specialised cancer hospital, the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, named after his mother, in Lahore. The hospital opened in 1994.That personal following later became the foundation of a political movement, the PTI, that presented him as an outsider challenging Pakistan’s established political order. In a country where civilian politics has long been shaped by the Bhutto-Zardari and Sharif families, Imran Khan offered voters a figure outside the traditional political dynasties. His image as a retired cricket captain with no family legacy in politics helped distinguish him from the established political class.His prime ministership brought him further visibility and established him as a central figure in Pakistan’s civilian politics.And therein lies his significance: an outsider who challenged Pakistan’s established political dynasties, became prime minister, and later fell out with the military establishment before being jailed.Pakistan’s 2024 general election offered the clearest indication that Imran Khan’s imprisonment had not erased his political relevance. Despite the PTI being stripped of its election symbol and Imran Khan remaining in prison, PTI-backed independents won 92 directly elected National Assembly seats — more than candidates backed by any other political grouping.While that result did not bring the party back to power, it showed that his absence from the ballot did not translate into the disappearance of his support.However, the outcome should not have been a surprise. In October 2022, just months after his ouster as prime minister, Imran Khan contested by-elections in seven of eight National Assembly constituencies voting on October 16. He won six of the seven seats he contested, while the Pakistan People’s Party won the other two constituencies.He then won another by-election in Kurram on October 30, taking his tally of by-election victories that month to seven.The by-election results offered an early indication that removing Imran Khan from office had not dented his electoral support. The 2024 elections reinforced that point, showing that his imprisonment and the restrictions placed on the PTI had not eliminated its support among voters.As its founder and most prominent face, PTI has repeatedly described Imran Khan as its “red line.” The phrase took on greater significance after his arrest on May 9, 2023, when Pakistan witnessed widespread rioting and arson by PTI supporters. Protesters targeted government buildings and military installations, including the residence of a corps commander in Lahore and the army’s general headquarters in Rawalpindi.The events marked a dramatic escalation in the confrontation between Imran Khan and the military establishment. They also demonstrated why the PTI has continued to place him at the centre of its politics: attempts to remove him from the political arena have not removed the attachment to him among a significant section of the party’s supporters.Since his incarceration, the party has repeatedly mobilised in Islamabad, demanding his release. The federal government’s frustration with these protests was evident ahead of the recently postponed Islamabad march, when interior minister Mohsin Naqvi spoke of the need to find a “permanent solution” to the PTI’s repeated demonstrations in the capital.“This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway,” Naqvi said.Therefore, Imran Khan remains the PTI’s “red line” — one reason efforts to marginalise him politically have so far struggled to succeed.Imran Khan’s prolonged imprisonment has also strengthened a persecution narrative around him. His party and supporters have consistently argued that the numerous cases against him are politically motivated and intended to keep him out of politics. Pakistani authorities have rejected those allegations.The fact that more than 100 cases have been brought against him, his disqualification by the Election Commission in 2022, and the restrictions imposed on the PTI ahead of the 2024 general elections have only strengthened that narrative among his supporters.The conditions of his imprisonment at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail have added another dimension to the persecution narrative.In December 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards raised concerns over reports that Khan was being held in conditions falling below international standards for humane and dignified detention. The communication cited allegations of prolonged solitary confinement, restricted access to the outside world and inadequate ventilation.Edwards subsequently urged Pakistani authorities to end his reported solitary confinement and ensure that his detention conditions complied with international standards, warning that the reported conditions could amount to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment.The Pakistani establishment has succeeded in keeping Imran Khan behind bars. But with so many eyes on his case, it has not succeeded in making his political relevance disappear.The controversy surrounding Imran Khan’s imprisonment has increasingly extended beyond politics and Pakistan, as his cricketing legacy has kept his case in the international spotlight.Former international cricket captains have appealed to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government over Khan’s treatment and access to medical care. In August, 21 former captains urged the government to ensure “humane treatment and proper medical care” for their former on-field rival.Matters almost came to a head during the recent England-Pakistan Test series. During the second Test at Lord’s, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly considered not sending its players back onto the field after the lunch break after Sky Sports aired an interview with Imran Khan’s sons, Kasim and Suleiman.The PCB ultimately returned to the field and lodged a complaint with the broadcaster.The episode underscored how Imran Khan’s imprisonment continues to attract attention beyond Pakistan and outside politics.Every time the PTI has marched on Islamabad, the Pakistan government has responded by fortifying the capital, blocking entry routes and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.Ahead of the September 27 march, authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and erected extensive barricades and roadblocks around Islamabad.The crackdown extended to Imran Khan’s family too, with his three sisters detained ahead of the now-postponed march.Such measures may prevent protesters from reaching Islamabad, but they have not stopped the PTI from returning to the streets with the same central demand: Imran Khan’s release. The state has managed to contain individual protests, but each confrontation has been followed by another, keeping his imprisonment at the centre of Pakistan’s politics.By isolating him in prison and cracking down on his family and party, the Pakistani authorities have sought to contain Imran Khan’s political influence. So far, however, his electoral support, PTI’s continued mobilisation and the attention surrounding his imprisonment show that those measures have not removed him from the country’s political contest.For now, Imran Khan’s ability to retain political relevance despite his imprisonment remains a significant feature of Pakistan’s politics.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023. He has faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics.

Article Title: BLF’s newly-formed female unit 'KAAD' attacks military convoy in Balochistan; claims nine killed
Article Text:
Image credit: X

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has released footage of an attack by its newly formed female unit on a Pakistani military convoy in Turbat, claiming that nine security personnel were killed in the operation.The video, released through the group’s media cell Aashoob, shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway on September 22.The footage includes a female commander briefing fighters before the operation, along with training clips. It also shows the fighters opening fire on the convoy from close range. The group claimed that several military vehicles were severely damaged and that several personnel were injured. These claims could not be independently verified.BLF spokesperson Major Gwahram Baloch said the group’s Qurban unit supported the operation and helped its fighters resist an attempt by Pakistani forces to encircle them, while covering their withdrawal. He said Qurban unit fighter Chakar Murad, alias Dileep Jan, was killed during the attack.The video also shows KAAD members conducting snap checks of vehicles in the Mangchar area of Kalat. The BLF claimed that its fighters carried out a blockade and vehicle checks there.In a separate incident, the Baloch Republican Army (BRA) claimed responsibility for an attack on a Mari Energies Limited site in the Beh Loti area of Dera Bugti, using rockets and heavy weapons.BRA spokesperson Sarbaz Baloch claimed that three company employees were killed and several others injured. He said a clash followed between Pakistani forces and members of a local armed group. The BRA claimed nine Pakistani military personnel and three members of the armed group were killed, while six of its own fighters also lost their lives, according to The Balochistan Post.The Baloch Republican Guards (BRG) separately claimed that its fighters seized Haji Shehr and destroyed a local police station using explosives. It also said BRA fighters entered Eri Shehr, took control of government facilities and withdrew after the operation.KAAD is named after Karima Baloch, a pro-independence activist and the first woman chairperson of the Baloch Students Organisation-Azad. She was found dead in Toronto in 2020.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) claims nine security personnel were killed in the operation. Video shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China- Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway.

Article Title: 'Technical issue': Pakistan blocks airspace for Russian flight carrying uranium for Bangladesh nuclear plant
Article Text:
Russia’s uranium shipment for Bangladesh’s Rooppur nuclear plant delayed (Image credit: Reuters)

Poll Vote & Share your view Should international diplomatic norms allow for expedited clearance of flights carrying critical supplies like nuclear fuel? Definitely Not at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has denied airspace clearance to a Russian cargo flight carrying nuclear fuel for Bangladesh's Rooppur nuclear power plant, delaying the scheduled arrival of uranium for the facility's Unit 2. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions.The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date, according to Bangladesh officials as cited by news agency ANI."We heard that a cargo plane carrying uranium for the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Bangladesh was scheduled to arrive on September 24. However, the flight was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace, so the uranium did not arrive in Bangladesh as planned. As of now, the exact reason for Pakistan not granting the airspace clearance is still unknown", ANI quoted Bangladesh's minister for science and technology Faqir Mahbub Anam saying."A new date has been proposed, with Russia indicating the first week of October for the uranium to arrive in Bangladesh", he added.Sheikh Mohammed Tauhidul Islam, joint secretary in Bangladesh's science and technology ministry, said preparations had been completed at the airport before officials were informed that the airspace was unavailable."We had completed all the preparations at the airport and were waiting, but the liaison officer from Rosatom told us that the airspace was not clear. So we couldn’t send it. It may need to be rescheduled", he said.Pakistan's high commission in Dhaka, in a clarification, said the matter was related to technical and procedural arrangements."Pakistan maintains an unwavering commitment to international diplomatic norms and processes all requests for diplomatic flight and overflight clearances within a standardised, predictable timeframe, strictly in accordance with our established regulatory guidelines and civil aviation protocols," ANI quoted it as saying."With regard to the reports being quoted, the matter appears to relate to technical and procedural arrangements concerning flight routing and airspace permissions, which can occasionally require coordination among the relevant aviation and other authorities and may result in adjustments to flight schedules", it added.The high commission also said the incident should not be linked to Pakistan-Bangladesh ties."Pakistan attaches high importance to its relations with Bangladesh, and it would therefore be appropriate to view the matter in its proper technical context and not attach undue significance to reports or narratives that may seek to misplace it to undermine our bilateral relations," it said.The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, Bangladesh's first nuclear power facility, is being built with technical assistance from Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom. The project comprises two VVER-1200 reactor units with a combined capacity of 2,400 MW.
Article Summary: The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date.

Article Title: 'Took mobile phones, cash': Karachi football team robbed at gunpoint on Balochistan highway
Article Text:
Image credit X @Baloch_Nojawan

NEW DELHI: A football team travelling from Karachi to Quetta to participate in the Chief Minister’s Gold Cup tournament was robbed at gunpoint on a highway in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, PTI reported on Monday.Around a dozen armed men intercepted the Karachi District West team’s bus between Mastung and Sariab, and took away the players’ mobile phones, cash and other valuables. The incident took place on Monday evening, leaving the players without money.Team manager Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto said the armed men ordered all passengers to get off the bus before robbing them."The armed men asked all the passengers to disembark from the bus and then took away all mobile phones, cash, and other valuables.
